subtopic: AGREED DECLARATION BY THE UNITED STATES, THE UNITED KINGDOM AND CANADA '

speechtext:
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs): Mr. Speaker, the Department of External Affairs has just received over the wire the text of a declaration signed this morning by the President of the United States, the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom and the Prime Minister of Canada, and I think it will be of interest to hon. members to have the text of this declaration at once. It is as follows:
Atomic Energy Agreed Declaration by the President of the United States,
the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, and
the Prime Minister of Canada
The President of the United States, the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, and the Prime Minister of Canada, have issued the following statement:
1.	We recognize that the application of recent scientific discoveries to the methods and practice of war has placed at the disposal of mankind means of destruction hitherto unknown, against
which there can be no adequate military defence, and in the employment of which no single nation can in fact have a monopoly.
2.	We desire to emphasize that the responsibility for devising means to ensure that the new discoveries shall be used for the benefit of mankind, instead of as a means of destruction, rests not on our nations^ alone, but upon the whole civilized world. Nevertheless, the progress that we have made in the development and use of atomic energy demands that w-e take an initiative in the matter, and we have accordingly met together to consider the possibility of international action:
(a)	to prevent the use of atomic energy for destructive purposes;
(b)	to promote the use of recent and future advances in scientific knowledge, particularly in the utilization of atomic energy, for peaceful and humanitarian ends.
3.	We are aware that the only complete protection for the civilized -world from the destructive use of scientific knowledge lies in the prevention of war. No system of safeguards that can be devised will of itself provide an effective guarantee against production of atomic weapons by a nation bent on aggression. Nor can we ignore the possibility of the development of other weapons, or of new methods of warfare, which may constitute as great a threat to civilization as the military use of atomic energy.
4.	Representing, as we do, the three countries which possess the knowledge essential to the use of atomic energy, we declare at the outset our willingness, as a first contribution, to proceed with the exchange of fundamental scientific inlormation and the interchange of scientists anu scientific literature foT peaceful ends with any nation that will fully reciprocate.
5.	We believe that the fruits of scientific research should be made available to all nations, and that freedom of investigation and free interchange of ideas are essential to the progress of knowledge. In pursuance of this policy, the basic scientific information essential to the development _of atomic energy for peaceful purposes has already been made available to the world. It is our intention that all further information of this character that may become available from time to time shall be similarly treated. We trust that other nations will adopt the same policy, thereby creating an atmosphere of reciprocal confidence in which political agreement and cooperation will flourish.
G. We have considered the questioii of the disclosure of detailed information concerning the practical industrial application of atomic energy. The military exploitation of atomic energy depends, in large part, upon the same methods and processes as would be required for industrial uses.
We are not convinced that the spreading of the specialized information regarding the practical application of atomic energy, before it is possible to devise effective, reciprocal, and enforceable safeguards acceptable to all nations, would contribute to a constructive solution of the problem of the atomic bomb. On the contrary, we think it might have the opposite effect. We are, however, prepared to share, on a reciprocal basis with others of the united nations, detailed information concerning the practical industrial application of atomic energy just as soon as effective enforceable safeguards against its use for destructive purposes can be devised.

Atomic Energy-Agreed Declaration
7.	In order to attain the most effective means of entirely eliminating the use of atomic energy for destructive purposes and promoting its widest use for industrial and humanitarian purposes, we are of the opinion that at the earliest practicable date a commission should be set up under the united nations organization to prepare recommendations for submission to the organization.
The commission should be instructed to proceed, with the utmost dispatch and should be authorized to submit recommendations from time to time dealing with separate phases of its work.
in particular, the commission should make specific proposals:
(a)	for extending between all nations the exchange of basic scientific information for peaceful ends,
(b)	for control of atomic energy to the extent necessary to ensure its use only for peaceful purposes,
(c)	for the elimination from national armaments of atomic weapons and of all other major weapons adaptable to mass destruction,
(d)	for effective safeguards by way of inspection and other means to protect complying states against the hazards of violations and evasions.
8.	The work of the commission should proceed by separate stages, the successful completion of each one of which will develop the necessary confidence of the world before the next stage is undertaken. Specifically it is considered that the commission might well devote its attention first to the wide exchange of scientists and scientific information, and as a second stage to the development of full knowledge concerning natural resources of raw materials.
3. Faced with the terrible realities of the application of science to destruction, every nation will realize more urgently than before the overwhelming need to maintain the rule of law among nations and to banish the scourge of war from the earth. This can only be brought about by giving wholehearted support to the united nations organization, and by consolidating and extending its authority, thus creating conditions of mutual trust in which all peoples will be free to devote themselves to the arts of peace. It is our firm resolve to work without reservation to achieve these ends.
The City of Washington,
The White House,
November 15, 1945.
Harry S. Truman President of the United States C. R. Attlee
Prime Minister of the United Kingdom W. L. Mackenzie King Prime Minister of Canada

Mr. ST. LAURENT: I have nothing to add to the declaration. It puts emphasis on the declared intent of the president and the two prime ministers to promote the setting up of a commission. I would assume that all concrete proposals recommended by the com-

subtopic: AGREED DECLARATION BY THE UNITED STATES, THE UNITED KINGDOM AND CANADA '
speechtext:
We have just listened to what I believe can be regarded as an historic statement, and I am sure that hon. members on every side of the house welcome it.
Only last evening I was reading the addresses which have been given recently by Professor Oliphant of Brimingham university, on the subject of atomic energy. The other day I was reading some of the statements which were issued by scientists in the United States, and the statement we have just heard is, I believe, in accordance with the feeling of the scientists whose experiments assisted in the discovery of atomic knowledge and its application to purposes of destruction. I believe that the emphasis placed by the statement of the three leaders on the reciprocal exchange of scientific information among all nations is well received by this parliament and that it will be so received by the world. I want to express my pleasure' at hearing this statement. I want to do something else: I want to extend congratulations to our own Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), to the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, and to the President of the United States upon the unanimous decision they have thus reached.

speechtext:
This is the fiftieth day of the session and the house has had no opportunity of discussing a $400,000 item for external affairs. I contended the other day that before parliament approves any more treaties, no matter of what description, there should be a constitutional change. We had an example of the unsatisfactory state of affairs in the interval between the two wars, when Canada was bound at Locarno by the Kellogg note, and by other considerations that became a matter of treaty. Certain covenants of the league of nations and others were also agreed to, over the head of parliament while parliament was in session; as a result of that policy we passed certain sanctions affecting Ethiopia and Italy, and then Canada was forced to annul them. I said the other day, in connection with civil aviation, that there should be a constitutional change that would prevent any minister of the crown from acting extraterritorially in the signing of agreements and protocols and treaties while parliament is 47696-I35J
in session, or without parliament first being called upon to pass upon such matters. There are no doubt similar treaties with some of the other dominions and the United States on this very matter.
Altogether I object to the way that external affairs business is being conducted over the head of parliament. We are supposed to follow the practice that obtains in the parliament of Great Britain. There they had a long debate on the atomic bomb and long debates on matters akin to this, and such matters are being discussed in the House of Commons there all the time. Here we are in the fiftieth day of the session faced with a treaty which will bind this country, while other financial treaties may involve us in millions of dollars in the years to come. I object to this sort of thing. I repeat, there should be a constitutional change to provide that no minister of the crown shall have the right to sign any treaty without reference to parliament. As the minister stated the other day, according to the British North America Act, 1867, parliament consists of the queen, the Senate and the House of Commons, and we have no information about this treaty. There was a short discussion last spring but I have never seen the treaty.

maintopic: TRANSPORT ACT, 1938 JURISDICTION OVER CERTAIN WATER CARRIERS IN MACKENZIE RIVER AREA

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, November 14, consideration of the motion of Mr. Chevrier for the second reading of bill No. 32, to amend the Transport Act, 1938.

maintopic: TRANSPORT ACT, 1938 JURISDICTION OVER CERTAIN WATER CARRIERS IN MACKENZIE RIVER AREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one who has surveyed the Mackenzie river valley and the adjacent territory on several occasions I feel it my duty to pass some comment on the bill introduced yesterday by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier). First as one who has a very warm feeling for the great north country, comprising approximately one million square miles, I want to compliment the minister on bringing the bill into the house. I am sure that the people living in the area up and down the whole Mackenzie river and its tributaries, the mining men, the prospectors and the business men, will all take hope out of the purposes of this bill.
In a brief but important statement the minister indicated that the chief difficulty to be overcome to-day is to be found in the high freight rates on goods going into and coming out of that country, and with that I agree. He mentioned particularly the rail rate from Edmonton to Waterways, the southern terminus of navigation on that route, and particularly the water rate now being charged on oil. Both are detrimental to the expansion and development of that great country. If the country is opened up, as it can be and will be if the freight rates are lowered and transportation facilities increased and improved, I can see a substantial development in that country.
If I were a citizen of Edmonton, that great city of the middle north, I should feel proud of the possibilities for that city which might result from an adjustment and improvement in freight rates and transportation facilities. Edmonton has to-day a population of something like 150.000, but having travelled through that area and knowing some of its potentialities I should be surprised if in due course it did not become a city with a population of 250,000 or 300,000.
I want to thank the minister for his earnestness in presenting this bill. I also want to say a word about the few remarks made by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church). I am always amazed at the hon. member's grasp of public affairs and his intimate knowledge of their details. He is a most indefatigable worker and I for one always like to hear him. He always presents something pertinent to the question. He said yesterday that water route rates are not under the control of the Department of Transport. I hope the minister will see to it that water route rates everywhere throughout Canada come under the control of the department, because water routes have a great deal to do with the development of the country.
It is not my intention to speak at any great length, but I feel that I should say something about the north country, and particularly the Mackenzie river valley. Paragraph (hh), which is to be added to the Transport Act reads as follows:
"Mackenzie river" means all rivers, streams, lakes and other waters within the watershed of the Mackenzie river.
The Mackenzie river basin is wholly within the boundaries of Canada. It is the largest river wholly within any one country in America. The Mississippi river is not wholly within the United States. The Milk river, one of its source tributaries, flows through Canada. The Mackenzie river is wholly within Canada and drains an area of about 525.000 square miles. It is the longest fresh water route in the world. I believe the total fresh water route on the Mackenzie is well on to 3.500 miles, if one takes in the length of the water route on lake Athabaska. Great Slave lake, Great Bear lake and the Peace river. From Hudson Hope on the Peace river, one of the most beautiful little hamlets I have ever seen, at the end of the great Peace river rapids to its mouth on the Rocher river, where with the Rocher it forms the Slave river, is a distance of at least six hundred miles, and every mile of that six hundred miles is navigable with the exception of four miles at Vermilion chutes, about which I shall say a word in a few minutes. Then there is a four hundred mile safe water route on a tributary, the Liard river, right up to Port Nelson. This is the longest fresh water route in the world, barred only at two places, at Vermilion chutes and at the rapids between Fort Fitzgerald and Fort Smith. So this river, its tributaries and its basin are of major importance in the development of this country.
Transport Act

This bill has to do with freight rates. Freight itself is vitally important to any transportation company operating in that area, and the only way they can lower their rates is through the development of new business. That area is open to the greatest potential new business I know of anywhere in America, and I have been over a great deal of it. It is the last great mineral area in the world. Yesterday the minister mentioned Yellowknife. When I visited Yellowknife there were seven gold-producing mines there, several of them very rich in ore. There is the Con mine; there is Yellowknife itself; there is the Negus mine operated by a group in Toronto of which I believe Hon. Charles McCrea is president; the Thompson-Lunmark mine; the Great Slave Lake mine, and others all round about, and so far they have only scratched the area. When any hon. member of the House of Commons visits the town of Yellowknife he will be surprised. It is a thriving, businesslike centre, and all through that area I saw vast amounts of equipment made down here in the east. So I know the factories of Ontario can increase their production and give more employment as that country is opened up. For that reason I am strongly behind any programme to lower the freight rates in that country, which to-day are altogether too high.
The Yellowknife area contains a great many gold mines, and further east along the north shore of Great Slave Lake whither I had planned to go but could not get transportation, I am told is located the largest bench of spodumene, the ore from which lithium comes, anywhere in America. If that is the case it will not be long until that is developed. Then further north up the Coppermine river, where there is the most beautiful falls anyone could see, which rejoice in the not very euphonious name of Bloody Falls-perhaps that name will be changed later-the country is full of copper. Up there I met representatives of one of the greatest copper companies in America. I talked with their engineers, and they told me the potentialities were tremendous. They were speaking of taking the copper out to the Arctic ocean and by boat from there around Cape Barrow, away up at the far northern corner of Alaska.
I must not delay the house longer talking about the vast potentialities of that country in regard to mineral wealth. It is also known everywhere for fish and for power. Bight now they send the fish from Great Bear lake and Great Slave lake by plane to Waterways and from there to Chicago and New York; and the demand is so great they cannot fill it. Those lakes are full of fish, wonderful

fish. I was greatly surprised at the Great Bear lake fish. They are hard but they taste sweet; an amazing fish. I have no doubt that as time goes on, if the lakes can continue to supply those fish, a great trade will be developed in flying fish out from that area. That is all new wealth. As for power, there are several magnificent power sites. The Slave river power is good for half a million horsepower; the Sans Souci rapids on the Mackenzie river I should say would be good for several million horse-power; the falls on the Hay river, which are 106 feet high, are good for a great deal of power. The whole country is full of vast power possiblities. If we as Canadians can only wake up to the opening of that country and its development, as is our heritage,. I can see a vast amount of -business coming out of it for plants down here in Ontario, Quebec and elsewhere. It can also- mean a great deal to the growth of its great focal point, the city of Edmonton. There is no telling how large Edmonton will grow if that country is opened up as it should be.
To-day, however, the freight rates hold it back. The minister said the rate on oil today is $30 a ton. That is 15 cents a gallon, or just about twice as much in freight as the oil is worth at Norman Wells; for I believe they told me they were selling bunker oil, which is what the minister referred to, at about six or more cents a gallon. It may have gone up since then, but when- they were selling gasoline at 28 cents a gallon, six to ten cents would be a normal price for bunker oil. Well, sir, if they are paying a freight rate of 15 cents a gallon on bunker oil it is too high,. The minister said the rate had been $20 a ton but to-day apparently it is $30. That is a fifty per cent increase in the freight rate, and certainly that is too much without the transport board inquiring into whether or not that should be the proper rate. I cannot believe that Imperial Oil would charge that much, because they were very wise; they purchased quite a number of United States steel barges, and got them at a low rate. I discussed the matter with the colonel in charge of United States equipment at Waterways, and my memory is that he said he would sell those barges for $17,000 each. That figure may be too low; it should not be taken as accurate, but that is my memory. Too many of those barges were cut to pieces with acetylene torches and shipped out of the country.
I did my best to create public sentiment for the purchase of those barges, and the same in regard to United States tugs. The Mackenzie river never had barges or tugs that

Transport Act
were equal to the tugs and barges the United States government used on that river during the war. They sent them up there because they could not be bothered with the slow dispatch of business on the river. The tugs were of the tunnel type, with the wheel coming up underneath in the centre, thereby protecting it against damage from sand bars or rocks. I am certainly sorry if very many of those tugs and barges were sent out of the country. They were for sale and should have been kept here, and I congratulate Imperial Oil on having purchased some of them. The matter of transportation is very important, and these big barges and fast tugs would help.
I say this in a friendly way, but I should like the minister and the Minister of Public Works or any other minister having to do with assisting traffic on the river to pay a visit there. Go together; you will enjoy your trip. Go down by boat and come out by air. You will have a wonderful trip down the river from Waterways; you will find it a great- education. By air, of course, you will come out very quickly; you will do it in a day. It will take mtany days to go down, but you will enjoy every minute of it.
I want to point out to the minister how he can cut down freight rates, and then he can take up the matter with the minister in charge. In the first place the freight rate from Edmonton to Waterways is an outrage. It is 305 miles from Edmonton to Waterways by rail. I have nothing but compliments for the company for building the road. But when the railway arrives at Waterways it stops three miles short of Fort McMurray, at the junction of the Clearwater and Athabaska rivers. The town of Waterways grew up because the railway stopped at that point. The railway company should have been censured, and the board of railway commissioners also, for permitting that railway to stop three miles short of where it should have gone. Then the railway company was permitted to call this an uncompleted railroad and charge exorbitant freight rates. I have not the rates in mind, but I discussed the matter with shippers at Waterways and every one was loud in his condemnation of the prices charged to ship freight from Edmonton to Waterways. If I were an Edmontonian I would strenuously object to these freight rates, because they retard the growth of Edmonton by keeping down the development of the country to the north.
So much for the railway. The minister mentioned it yesterday and I hope he takes this matter under advisement. As I say, the freight rates from Edmonton to Waterways are far too high; they are a detriment to
business. This bill will give the transport commissioners authority to deal with the whole freight business in that country and I hope they will do what they can to see that this rate comes down.
From Waterways north, or from Fort McMurray, which is just three miles away, to Aklavik, is 1,660 miles. Aklavik itself is sixty miles south of the ocean. This town is located on the Peel river, which is part of the Mackenzie river delta. That is quite a distance, and the only obstruction on that whole route are the rapids at Fort Fitzgerald. When I went through that country I was humiliated that we had not done more to develop it. When the boat leaves Waterways it travels north for 287 miles before any obstruction is met. It then arrives at Fort Fitzgerald, where everything has to be dumped out and taken across a portage of sixteen miles. That is certainly not the way to build up this country. I must pay a great compliment to Ryan brothers, who operate over the portage, and also Northern Transportation, who now operate over the portage at Fort Fitzgerald to Fort Smith. But that does not detract from my statement of a moment ago that the obstruction which necessitates the portage should be eliminated.
There are two ways of doing this. A canal of about sixteen or perhaps eighteen miles could be built. I made the best survey I could as to where this canal could be built, and it would seem to be a simple engineering matter to canalize this area. Or we could follow the plan adopted by our American cousins when they arrived at Fort Fitzgerald. They were annoyed to such an extent at what they found that they sent up gigantic trucks upon which they could load their tugs and boats. The roadway was improved and by the means of tractors they were able to take these boats to Fort Smith. If they could do that, I do not see why we could not either build a canal or a marine railway. Then boats coming to Fort Fitzgerald from Waterways could continue to Fort Smith, either through the canal or over the marine railway, and get into the river at that point. If we had that, we would then have a route 1,660 miles long without an obstruction. That would be a credit to Canada.
That is one way to cut down the freight rates. Canada has done a lot for the rest of the country; not so much has been done for the north west. We have done a lot to help the east, and I am all for it, but I am going to go a little further and ask that help be given to the people of the west-and the far northwest. This is one way in which we can do something. This obstruction at Fort Fitz-
Transport Act

gerald could be eliminated so that commerce going north would not have to break bulk. That would help to bring down the freight rates, and I do not know of anything else that would do more to open up that country than a reduction of the freight rates.
At the same time the traffic would be speeded up. The Northern Transportation company owns two boats, the Northern King and the Northern Queen. The Northern Queen makes the trip from Waterways to Fort Fitzgerald and the Northern King runs north from Fort Smith to either Yellowknife or Fort Norman. I think it could go right down to Aklavik, but I do not know whether it does. The Northern King and the Northern Queen are both diesel engine boats. I went north to Fort Fitzgerald on the Northern Queen. The large Hudson's Bay company boats are not diesel engine boats, but I hope they will get this type of boat, because it permits of more speed and that is something we must have in that country. I do not want anyone to think that I am saying anything unkindly about the Hudson's Bay company. Far from it; because I have nothing but praise for their service and the pioneering work they have done in that country. They deserve unstinted praise for what they have done through the years in opening up that country without any help.
Once you are aboard the boat at Waterways you may have difficulty getting out of the harbour because of sand bars. Then when you get into the Athabaska river you at once run into further difficulties unless there is high water. First you must pass over a limestone ledge, and then there are sand bars to be avoided in the river. The sand bars should not be there, but they are, and the boats must zigzag from one side of the river to the other. You would be surprised at the circuitous route that must be followed. If that route could be shortened they would be able to cut down the freight rates.
When your ship comes close to Take Athabaska you find right in front of you what is known as the Embarras river, but the boat turns off to the right and travels about sixty miles before it enters lake Athabaska. I do not think it would be over five or ten miles at the most that you would have to travel to enter the lake through an Embarras route. You would then strike the lake at a point opposite Chipewyan. If an Embarras channel could be opened there by the Department of Public Works or whatever department has this matter under their control, there would be a saving of at least fifty miles and a consequent speeding up of traffic.

Then at the outlet of Great Slave lake, about forty miles west, there are some rapids which in low water give the shipping companies some difficulty. They can go up the rapids, but they have to pull themselves up. Then there are the Sans Souei rapids, which are about 100 miles northwest of Norman Wells. Here again they have to pull themselves up the rapids. Some hon. members may not be familiar with how this is done. They pick up a buoy attached to a cable in the water and wind the cable around the capstan. They then start the engine and in that way are able to pull the boat up the rapids.
The minister should interest himself in speeding up traffic on the river by the elimination of obstructions. A little while ago I referred to some small rapids on the Peace river about 200 miles west of its junction with the Rocher. This river flows out of lake Athabaska for about forty miles, and then the Peace river comes in and together they form the Slave. Two hundred miles up the Peace river-and sometimes I think the magnitude of these rivers is not appreciated- you come to Vermilion Chutes, fifty miles down the river from Fort Vermilion. Those chutes are only four miles long, with the water dropping twenty-four feet. We have owned that country since 1870, and it is amazing that those chutes have not been canalized. It is just an ABC job to go around those rapids, and if we did that, a boat from Hudson Hope, another four hundred miles up the river, could sail right down to Fort Fitzgerald, and if we had a canal there too it could sail right down to Aklavik. What would that mean? At Aklavik I was told they pay $140 a ton in freight on coal-and I can well believe it, because the boats coming in there are not equipped1 to carry coal and. carry only a few bags at a time. You cannot develop a country on a $140 a ton freight rate on coal. But if the Vermilion rapids were out of the way, and the rapids at Fort Fitzgerald, Hudson Hope coal, which could be bought at Hudson Hope for five or six or seven or eight dollars a ton-that may be too low or too high- could be transported at a freight rate from Hudson Hope to Aklavik that would be a mere bagatelle compared with the rate to-day. That is another point I wish the minister to take note of, because the people there must have coal or oil, and that brings up the point the minister mentioned about oil.
There is a good market in that country for oil stoves. I found many people there using a stove-I have forgotten the name, but it is like the stove sold in Toronto by the Addison industry. The minister will know that industry because it did a big job during the war.

Transport Act
I saw one of these stoves in Doctor Livingstone's house at Aklavik, and in the hospital there, and all the people who have used it have great praise for it. Perhaps that far north country can be taken care of by oil from Norman Wells, and if it can, well and good. On the other hand they must be able to buy these stoves at a reasonable rate, and the present package freight rate is away too high. I hope that as a result of this bill the conditions will improve. In any event, the far north country will be a big market for stoves made down in the east. I do not know where the Addison company makes its stove. The Coleman company also makes a similar stove, and there may be other companies. Perhaps I should not have mentioned any names, but I have mentioned these two lines because they are examples of what other companies may be doing. Thirty dollars a ton for fuel oil is too high if we are going to build up any country. We should do all we can to reduce the freight rate and to develop a faster and safer route to the north.
There is one other thing. The minister may know that the Mackenzie river is open to navigation about the middle of May or earlier from Great Slave lake almost to the mouth of the river. That may seem incredible, but it is so. But Great Slave lake itself is not open until July. The summer I went down there by boat

maintopic: TRANSPORT ACT, 1938 JURISDICTION OVER CERTAIN WATER CARRIERS IN MACKENZIE RIVER AREA
speechtext:
That is roughly 400 miles south of Great Slave lake. Great Slave lake is frozen solid almost up to the 1st of July, and the Hudson Bay company boats when they reach Great Slave lake have to wait until the lake ice has moved out. If my hon. friend will read the life of Sir Alexander Mackenzie and other great explorers he will recall that when they arrived at Great Slave lake they were compelled to wait quite a long time for a channel to open up to the river itself. There is a way to overcome that. I doubt if human beings can overcome the freezing of Great Slave lake or have it opened up earlier, but certainly it does retard navigation on the river to have the lake frozen solid until the summer. But last winter and for several winters before a tractor train has gone out from Peace river via Grimshaw up to Notikewin. Up to that point there is a good road, and from there north a tractor
road. The Alberta government and the federal government, I am' glad to say, are now going to make a good road from Notikewin via Alexandra falls, which is a very beautiful falls on the Hay river, a fall of 106 feet, where by and by a lot of power will be developed. Then the road will branch off, with one road going up from the mouth of the Hay river and across the lake to Yellowknife. The village is called Hay River too. I stopped at Hay River to see all I could. Northwest from Alexandria Falls the other branch goes to Mills Lake, which is just a post, forty miles west of Fort Providence, west of the lake called Mills lake. When I refer to Mills Lake I am referring to the post, not to the lake.
At Mills Lake there is a tractor winter road across the Mackenzie river, and after another 400 miles or thereabouts you arrive at Norman Wells. Norman Wells to my mind must be supported. It is a fine centre. There is a lot of business there. I was pleased to see there all kinds of stuff that I knew SO' well that had been made down here in the east. That is what I am interested in, the market potentialities, because it means more employment down east, more employment in the minister's own fine city of Cornwall, more employment in the fine city of Peterborough represented so ably by the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser), and more employment in Mr. Deputy Speaker's own fine manufacturing city of Brantford. I could go on and name many other fine cities, including Ottawa too, and round about, all of which would benefit by development of that far north country. We are shipping annually 25,000 tons of freight down that river even at the present high freight rate, and you can readily picture 200,000 tons of freight going down that river if we had a reasonable freight rate. What would that mean to employment in old Ontario and Quebec, yes, and in Winnipeg too, where they have a lot of fine plants? It would mean more business of every description all over the country.
I hope that the minister's bill will result in opening up that country through the cutting down of freight rates, which are altogether too high to-day, and in the development of business. That is the only objective I have in mind, and the minister will receive my hearty support for any programme that he can outline which will do these two things-increase the speed of traffic up and down the river and cut down the freight rate on the river, and see to it that the people up in that country who need oil for fuel for heating hospitals, schools and their homes are not charged at the rate of $30 a ton.

Transport Act

Just four hundred miles down the river is Norman Wells. At that point there are, I believe, some fifty wells which flow oil. They opened the Canol pipeline to let it flow, and have had success in producing up to three thousand barrels of oil per day; in fact, on one occasion nearly eight thousand barrels were produced in a day. The oil is there, and the Imperial Oil sell it at a low rate. They could charge a lot more if they wanted to, but to their credit the rate they charge is very reasonable.
Do not retard the country bv allowing transport companies to charge exorbitant rates, and then the minister will make a name for himself, and he will become a lover of the north country, as I am. I can hardly leave it when I go there; in fact it is a tourist's paradise; there is nothing like it in the world. I dreamed two months after I left Aklavik of the Mackenzie delta, the most weird and amazing spectacle I have ever seen, worth anyone's visit. Between freight and tourist traffic this country will reap a rich harvest and do a great deal for the world and for Canada.
Mr. HARRY R. JACKMAN (Rosedale): Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is apparently simple enough-merely to place under the Department of Transport the fixing of rates on the Mackenzie river area; but I fail to see how it really strikes at the root of the matter.
We have had an interesting description of the area by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol), from which I think we may realize that this area is a somewhat peculiar one as far as shipping concerned. I should be glad if the minister at some time during the discussion would say whether or not there are any similar areas under the jurisdiction, of the board of transport commissioners at the present time. For instance, the freeze-up comes early, and there is somewhat less than six months of open water for these shipping facilities to use. Where else in Canada are there similar transportation difficulties where the rates are fixed by the board of transport commissioners?
If the minister should think I am critical of this bill, it is not that I am, but that I feel we should have certain information and find out exactly whether the objective which he seeks, and which is an excellent one, is to be achieved by the passing of such a measure as this.
In the minister's introductory remarks he mentioned that of the three shipping companies plying this route, one was owned by the dominion government through the acquisi-

tion of the Eldorado Mining company. When the auditor general investigated the profit and loss statement of that shipping company he decided that the rate of $20 per ton was not enough for bunker fuel oil, and the rate was therefore raised by a government department to no less than $30. Apparently there was a certain amount of complaint from shippers, and it would seem that the solution is merely to refer this whole matter to the board of transport commissioners, a government body, the government already having decided that a subsidy is not in order. And may I say that, whereas the northbound traffic is of a nature which seemingly can stand the tariff, the southbound traffic, which consists entirely of pitchblende and fuel oil, is of such a nature- at least, with reference to pitchblende, a product massive in nature and heavy in weight-that it cannot bear a very heavy tariff. Therefore fuel oil, the one item which can bear such a tariff, is obviously charged a rate which will help to balance accounts; and as I have already said, a government-owned shipping company could not get along with a S20 rate and had to raise it to $30.
I am wondering where in this present bill is a solution. What is the principle upon which rates will be set? Where is the magic which the board of transport commissioners can exercise which cannot be exercised if matters are left to themselves? If the returns at the present time are large-and as I have already pointed out, the auditor general has said that they have been in the red rather than in the black-new capital will be attracted to shipping on this route and new ships will thereby be provided; competition will therefore adjust the rate to that which is fair. I do not see why the government should assume to adjust these difficulties when they can be adjusted by the normal process of open competition, particularly at the present time, when capital is going begging and looking for places where it can get, not necessarily a high return, but any kind of fair return. If there is a genuine economic complaint on the part of some of the shippers, may I point out that those shippers, most of them being mining companies, -and some of them quite prosperous, are not impecunious. They can provide their own shipping, just as the Eldorado Mining company did, and it could be made a public vehicle and therefore forced to take any traffic which is offered. As I have said, when there is a sufficiency of ships, if there is an inordinate profit the rate will come down through the working of competition.
As I see it, this bill merely passes the buck; and unless the minister will explain to the house what principle is better than free com-

Transport Act
petition, I cannot see that the adoption of the bill will serve any useful purpose. As I see it, either the rates must be maintained at a level found necessary by the auditor general or by the private owners, or they must be subsidized. If the former, what useful function can the board of transport commissioners perform? If the latter, the Department of Transport will only have to refer the matter of the subsidy to this house for an appropriation. Therefore I would ask the minister just what solution is to be provided by passing the matter over to another government department rather than leaving it to the free play of the ordinary business enterprise of the country.

maintopic: TRANSPORT ACT, 1938 JURISDICTION OVER CERTAIN WATER CARRIERS IN MACKENZIE RIVER AREA
speechtext:
Last night the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) asked a number of questions in connection with the purport of this bill, and I should like to deal with these for a moment before coming to the remarks made by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) and the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman).
The hon. member for Broadview asked among other things over what water-borne traffic the board of transport commissioners have jurisdiction. The answer to that can be found in section 12 of the Transport Act, which this bill seeks to amend. Roughly speaking, it can be said that the board of transport commissioners have jurisdiction' over all water carriers on the great lakes and on the river St. Lawrence as far east as the western tip of the island of Orleans.
The hon. gentleman asked what policy the government had with reference to control over international and interprovincial traffic. That, as the hon. gentleman knows, is a moot question. Perhaps the best answer is to say that in 1937 the then Minister of Transport 'introduced in the senate a bill to amend the Transport Act, in which there was a section that had to do with the, control of interprovincial and international traffic so far as buses and motor trucks were concerned. The opposition to that section of the bill was such that in the final analysis the bill was defeated, so that the following year, when chapter 53, an act to establish the board of transport commissioners, was brought before the house, the section concerning control over interprovincial and international traffic was simply withdrawn from the bill.
Hon. members will know that the provinces maintain that they have jurisdiction not only over provincial motor traffic and vehicular traffic but also interprovincially. So that at this time to think of including in this bill con-47696- 136i
sideration of that subject matter without agreement with the provinces, would not I think be opportune.
The hon. gentleman asked what was being done by the board of transport commissioners during the war. The board have been continuing their sittings during the war just as they have done in peace. It is their business to inquire into and hear complaints and appeals under the railway act. This they have been doing and will continue to do. Much of their work however has been curtailed and restricted because of orders of the wartime prices and trade board. I can think at the moment of th question which the hon. member for Davenport raised when he complained vehemently-I do not blame him for that- about the freight rates charged from Edmonton to Waterways. Order No. 92 of wartime prices and trade board, which is a part of the general war policy, regulated the prices and rates charged for both goods and services, and regulated also freight rates; and it froze freight rates, in so far as that area and others are concerned, at the level at which they were in 1941.
While it may be that the work of the board has been curtailed by some war measures, it has also been extended because of the cooperation which the board of transport commissioners lend to the work of the transport controller, for instance, and it has among other things regulated and supervised the carriage of dangerous munitions of war and explosives.
The member for Davenport dealt at length with the purport of the bill, and I wish to thank him for the interesting remarks which he made, not only with reference to the bill itself, but on the subject of traffic in the whole northwest country, which he knows so well. I think the house will be grateful to him for the suggestions he has made. Those suggestions were aimed chiefly at speeding up the traffic in that great country which has so much potential mineral and other wealth.
The hon. member suggested several methods which, I must admit, this bill would not have the authority to implement. But I would say to him that, as he anticipated, I am greatly interested, and I am sure the Department of Transport is exceedingly interested in that whole north country. The Department of Public Works, as the hon. gentleman knows, has jurisdiction over the deepening of the channel. Already it has spent some small sums in deepening the channel in that area. The Department of Transport has jurisdiction over aids to navigation, but it has not spent large amounts of money, perhaps not as much as it should, possibly because perhaps of the distance of the Mackenzie river district.
Transport Act

Most of the work in connection with aids to navigation by the department has been performed through an agent of the Department of Mines and Resources in that area.
Freight rates, as I intimated! in my statement on the second reading, have been complained of as being too high. The member for Rosedale asks whether this is simply a process of passing the buck. The hon. member for Davenport has suggested some methods by which, over and above this, the problem can be met. I am prepared and willing to give consideration to these methods, but I ask the member for Rosedale, what other method is there under the circumstances, when a person complains about a high rate or the excessiveness of a rate, than to refer the whole matter to the body that has jurisdiction over such nates in Canada? And that body is the board of transport commissioners. It has the staff, engineers and men who over a period of years have become conversant with that work, know it, and have been doing it. It is not at all a question of passing the buck, but rather a question of bringing to the attention of the board the existence of an anomalous situation in that area.
The method which the board follows is this. Having been appraised of the situation it asks whether these carriers are prepared to file a tariff rate, after of course the act comes into force. I mean by that, that in the first instance these carriers must be licensed, and after they have obtained their licence to carry goods and passengers they file with the board a standard tariff of their tolls and charges for passengers and goods, be it package freight or goods in bulk. That tariff is posted in the offices of all the carriers in that area so that the public know in advance what the charges are, and should the charges be exorbitant or too high then the board has machinery to hear complaints. Having heard the complaints it may alter and reduce rates as it sees fit in accordance with the evidence which it hears. That has been the procedure of the board, and I think on the whole it has worked out fairly well.
All this bill seeks to do-while I should like to see it do more, as to the development of the resources of that great country and assistance to those who live there-in those circumstances, is to amend the Transport Act so as to bring water carriers in this whole northern area, the Mackenzie river district, within the jurisdiction of the board of transport, commissioners in order that they may regulate the carriers, their tariffs and their tolls. I think it is a good bill and I commend it to the house.

Section 2 covers the definition of a ship. Hon. members will have noted that in the Mackenzie river district that word includes a scow, and in other parts of Canada it includes a dredge. The board of transport commissioners have extensive powers over shipping. In some of the cities in Canada there is considerable difficulty with traffic by reason of the opening of bridges. In my home city of Vancouver we have what is known as False creek, which is an inlet extending into the heart of the city. There is very little shipping on that inlet. I have no wish to interfere with what actual shipping there is, that is, shipping in the ordinary sense, but every so often scows with derricks on them are brought into that inlet. While there is one high level bridge, there are three bridges that are not high level; they have tc be opened, and it sometimes causes the utmost confusion. speechtext:
May I say I am surprised that the minister should ask for special powers having to do with the regulation of the Mackenzie river area which are not applicable to shipments in bulk on the great lakes. May I say to my colleague, the hon. member for Davenport, thait I do not take second place to him in the wish that this northern country may be developed. However, I believe that development is more likely to come about if the board of transport commissioners are not given the power to fix rates. It may be that they will allow a return of so much per cent on the capital invested or a little higher rate, whatever it may be, but I believe the effective development of this great northern country could be better left to the working of free enterprise.	[DOT]
If there is a shortage of ships now and if the tariff, whether it be a tariff collected only from the shipper or a subsidized tariff paid in part by the government, is profitable, there will be sufficient ships of one sort or another to carry all the traffic that is offered and in that way develop the country. If the return
happens to be large for a few years or even for a year it will soon be found that in place of three shipping companies there will be half a dozen shipping companies. The ordinary course of competition will mean that the rates will be reduced.
The only hesitation I have in regard to putting this area of navigation under the Department of Transport is that it is a pioneer area and subject to certain hazards, such as the early freezing factor, and is therefore a field which does not lend itself, in the early stages, to regulation. When it is developed and one knows what operating conditions and costs will be, I dare say it could then come under the Department of Transport for the fixing of rates, as do other shipping routes. However, I would point out again to the committee that the Department of Transport do not seek to exercise jurisdiction over bulk shipments elsewhere in Canada; they only want it in this particular place.
If the desire of the hon. member for Davenport and of the whole committee is to be achieved, I think it would be better to leave this matter to the open forces of competition which would provide the necessary services. That competition in turn will be a most effective regulator of rates, whereas if you put it under the Department of Transport you will have the dead hand of regulation upon it and I believe that will have the effect of stifling the development of the north country.
