subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP PAYMENT OF $300,000 FOR FIVE YEARS ENDING JULY 1, 1949

speechtext:
Hon. ALPHONSE FOURNIER (Minister of Public Works) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a measure to authorize the Minister of Public Works on behalf of His Majesty, to enter into an agreement to pay to the Corporation of the City of Ottawa the sum of $300,000 annually for a period of five years from the first day of July, 1944, and for other purposes stated in the agreement.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this resolution precedes a bill which will be based on the recommendations of a special committee of the House of Commons and the Senate which was set up in 1944. For about ten years members of the house had been requesting that a committee be set up to hear representations which would be made by the city of Ottawa for an increase in the grant, which at that time was $100,000 a year. In 1942 the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) made that suggestion in the house, and also the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith), the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Boucher) and, I believe, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). After those representations had been made a committee was set up in May, 1944. The reference to the committee read as follows:
To review the special problems arising out of the location of the seat of government in the city of Ottawa and to report on the relations between the federal government and the municipal authorities of the said city and their relative responsibilities in respect to such problems, with power to inquire into the matter ana things therein referred to.
That committee met on many occasions. They heard evidence given by His Worship the Mayor of the city of Ottawa, by members of the board of control, by aldermen, by officials of the city, by members of the Ottawa board of trade, by members of the federal district commission and by the secretary of the Department of Public Works. After evidence had been brought before the committee, it was moved toward the end of the sittings, by the hon. member for Ottawa West, seconded1 by the hon. member for Carleton, that a grant of $500,000 be made to the city of Ottawa. That amendment did not carry, but the committee did adopt unanimously the suggestion that the grant be raised from $100,000 to $300,000 for civic services rendered to the government.
The bill will be based on that recommendation, which was only one of the recommendations made by that committee. The other

recommendations had1 to do with the federal district commission, with the extending of the territory to come under their jurisdiction and other matters. I believe that this resolution should be dealt with only as it pertains to the relations between the government and the city of Ottawa.
The last agreement with the city of Ottawa was dated March, 1920. In that agreement the government made a grant of $75,000 to the city for water services, water used for sprinkling streets and parkways belonging to the federal district commission or to the government, for fire protection, and1 probably for police protection. That grant was to be made for five years. In 1924, at the expiration of that agreement, negotiations were made to have the grant- increased but no agreement was reached at that time. In 1925 the1 amount was increased to $100,000, and the agreement made for five years. Then in- 1930 an agreement was made for one year only, and since then up to 1944 a bill has been introduced every year renewing the- agreement of 1920. Since 1920 conditions have changed quite a bit in the city of Ottawa through the purchase of property by the federal government, and the services rendered1 by the city have accordingly increased. The government believes that for this grant of $300,000 we receive benefits through the services rendered.
These agreements which have been passed by the house for a good many years are a consequence of section 125 of the British North America Act, which provides that lands and property belonging to the federal or provincial governments are not liable to taxation. At the time of confederation no request was made for any grant, but in 1877 the government signed a contract with the city of Ottawa for the use of the city's water and this amount has been modified or increased as the years have gone by. We pay for the water that is used in the public buildings; that is contained in one section of the agreement, as we shall see when we come to study the bill.
The bill has only one clause. It differs very little from the agreement of 1930 except as to the amount of the grant. There have been a few amendments made for clarification and for certain inducements, but the other provisions are very similar to those contained in previous agreements.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP PAYMENT OF $300,000 FOR FIVE YEARS ENDING JULY 1, 1949
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to call attention to what the minister said last session regarding this grant to the city of Ottawa. I am not opposing the vote at all because considering what the city of Ottawa has done I think $300,000 is not too much to grant annually

City of Ottawa Agreement
for a period of five years. But I do say this, that the principle of this vote was first adopted in 1917, following a report which I had prepared for the. city of Toronto long before this agreement ever came into being. What was that report? It produced a collection of data from all over the world as to what federal governments were doing for capital cities in the way of a subvention and bonuses or subsidies. It showed the account as between the city of Toronto and the federal government and between other cities in Canada and the federal government, and, second, it showed the account as between the largest cities of the province and the provincial government. As a result of that report Mr. Fisher, who was then mayor of Ottawa, a few years later, interviewed the government and an agreement was reached to make a grant to the city of Ottawa as a subvention given in exchange for municipal services of all kinds. It was made only locally for Ottawa instead of for all Canada.
I am not opposing this appropriation at all. Far from it. But I do say that various ministers, when this legislation has been up in other years, have indicated that some action might also be taken by the federal government with regard to other cities, with a view to paying the municipalities right across the country for similar municipal services rendered. In Toronto several millions of dollars worth of government property are exempt from taxation. For years in Toronto the government would not build a sidewalk or pay for a roadway built in front of their property. The principle of this appropriation is payment for municipal services rendered. The services rendered by the municipality to the federal government include not only water service but police and fire protection and other municipal services, and in Toronto the water services and other utilities services are supplied to the government at cost. Then there is also the building of roads, sewers and all that kind of thing. In 1905 the government of Sir James Whitney in Ontario first paid for the local improvements at the normal school there that were made on Church and Gerrard streets. They were the first government in the dominion to pay the municipalities for these improvements and they made it provincial wide. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) last year and the year before indicated-his words will be found in Hansard -that inquiry would be made and a survey made into the question of paying other cities and towns, urban and suburban and rural communities, for exactly the same kind of municipal services rendered to the government. When the war was on, look at the cost of
maintaining various public services! Take the municipal police and fire services, for example, and many other services. The onus has been placed on the municipality for enforcing federal law, and in that way the local authorities have been placed under a burden for years. The same thing runs through every federal department. Even the life-saving stations of Toronto supply services all over the lakes of Ontario and all their equipment is provided and maintained by the city.
Something should also be done about the intolerable conditions that prevail at the Ottawa union station. Everybody knows of the traffic congestion there and how the trains are held up. Somebody is going to be killed down at the station if nothing is done about it. Only the fine work of railway employees prevents it. Everybody has noticed the lack of protection there for the travelling public. The trains also come into the station by a roundabout way; many of them get in late, or early in the morning, and all that kind of thing.
Has the minister made any inquiry into the question of paying a subvention to other municipalities for the very same municipal services? Subvention was the word used in 1917 in the report which I have already mentioned, following which Mayor Fisher of Ottawa a few years later interviewed the federal government and secured a grant for the city of Ottawa. I was president of the union of municipalities at the time, and I know that the city of Ottawa, as a result of the report I mentioned, was the first city to have this principle adopted. In Australia, Sydney got $2,500,000 for maintaining the police force, and in the United States many municipalities on lake Erie to the head of the lakes, which maintain stations and aids to shipping receive a federal grant, as does the city of Detroit. We have nothing like that in Canada. Yet a large sum of money is collected by the government from the municipalities. Surely the government should read the handwriting on the wall and give some consideration to paying Vancouver, Winnipeg, Toronto, Hamilton, London, Saint John, Halifax, Quebec, Montreal and many other cities and towns in Ontario and across the country for similar municipal services rendered. Nobody is objecting to Ottawa being the capital city, but one thing I do object to is this. We have capable Canadian engineers, graduates of McGill, Laval, Western, university of British Columbia, Dalhousie university and others, who have helped to build the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Canadian National Railways and the Chippawa power canal, and who are quite
City oj Ottawa Agreement

capable of helping to build up this country in other ways. I am not objecting to anybody being brought from the old land or France to give advice, but they should be brought here to act in an advisory capacity only. We have many Canadian graduates who can tell them a lot more than some of those who have been brought here know. The United States acquired hundreds of our Canadian citizens as engineers in great works.
I urge upon the minister that he should do something about the federal district improvement commission. Last winter conditions were intolerable right in front of this parliament building and in these grounds. Something should be done to regulate the traffic around these buildings. In winter the streets on the hill here are impassable. Certainly at times in these grounds they are no credit to Canada, as I have said before.
The city of Ottawa is a very fine city, and Ottawa people are fine people in many ways. Still I maintain that the principle of this appropriation should be extended to include other cities and towns across Canada where similar services are performed for the government. For that reason, while I support this increase, on grounds of equality of treatment I urge that along these lines something be done for other cities.
I would also bring to the minister's attention the monuments around these buildings. Some stand in the front, some are in the back, and others are in the backyard by the coal bin of a great Irish statesman. I would ask that the attention of the federal district improvement commission be drawn to some of the points I have raised, and finally I urge that subventions be granted to other municipalities which are also supplying similar services at the expense of the local taxpayer, which imposes the burden on real estate in this country.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP PAYMENT OF $300,000 FOR FIVE YEARS ENDING JULY 1, 1949
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to take issue with the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), who has urged that the government consider subventions for other cities, but I would point out that this appropriation of $300,000 should not be considered a grant in any shape or form. It is actually an estimated compensation for services rendered. It is not a substitute for taxation.
Might I point out some of the facts which were revealed before the committee, whose report no doubt many hon. members have read. If the dominion government were to pay taxes on its property in Ottawa at the rate of assessments and of taxation city residents have to pay, calculating the taxation on the public school rate, not the separate school

rate, it would amount to $2,117,727.70 a year. That may indicate that the day is coming in Canada when the British North America Act should be amended so that the government, for any government-owned property, should compensate the municipalities in some way in lieu of taxation or render their property subject to taxation. Might I also point out that the annual assessment value of government-owned property in Ottawa in 1920, when the grant was originally set at $75,000, was $30 million. The assessed value of government-owned property in 1943, according to the best calculations, amounted to over $654 million. Those facts are cited only by way of some indication of the services which the municipality must render to the dominion government and its various enterprises.
I do not wish to delay the house in discussing this matter, because I believe a joint committee of both houses went into it in some respects thoroughly and were unanimous in their opinion that at least $300,000 should be granted. I should, however, like to point out that the government should implement this recommendation on a basis of five years rather than on that of an annual grant. That is only fair to the municipality, and should be approved by this house. I also wish to point out that it is paid1 direct to the city of Ottawa for services rendered by this city and paid for by its taxpayers, for government services of many kinds within the city, and that the position of the federal district is not involved.
I believe the government could very well afford to bring in the complete report of this committee and have it discussed in the house so far as the setting up of a federal area or a fedbral district is concerned. It would be very much to the advantage of Canada and of all hon. members if a discussion were had on the committee's report and as to the prospects of establishing a national capital area here. But I do not think these matters should enter into the present debate. The resolution merely proposes to give the city of Ottawa compensation for services rendered, and the wording of the motion indicates that it is so regarded' by the government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP PAYMENT OF $300,000 FOR FIVE YEARS ENDING JULY 1, 1949
speechtext:
I have not risen to oppose this measure. The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) mentioned a few minutes ago the case of Halifax. The situation there is in many ways unique. We have there tax exemptions to the extent of fifty per cent of the real property of the city. Of that fifty per cent, seventy iper cent is federally owned property. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) said in the house a few days ago that under the provisions of the British North America Act, section 125, no tax

City oj Ottawa Agreement
can. be levied on the property of Canada by either the dominion or a province. However, in 1867 when the act was passed, conditions in this country were vastly different from what they are now. At that time the total cost of municipal services was infinitesimal compared with what it is to-day.
There is another consideration which distinguishes the case of Halifax from that of the greater number of cities in the dominion. We have the Canadian National railway terminals on the Atlantic in Halifax, and the railways own a great deal of property in the city. Purely and solely by reason of the fact that the railway property there which is now owned by Canadian National Railways was formerly the property of the Intercolonial Railway company, it is tax exempt so far as Halifax is concerned. Things would be entirely different had it not been that it was the Intercolonial railway which Canadian National Railways absorbed. Had our railway property in Halifax been owned by the Grand Trunk instead of the Canadian Northern, the amount of tax exemption would have been very much less.
That is the situation in Halifax to-day. As hon. members know, the burden which was placed on that city in recent years, and which I am not going into this afternoon, has been enormous. I merely want to say this, that instead of opposing this motion I support it, and I think any agreement based on it and approved by this house may furnish a useful precedent for cities and municipalities that can make a strong case such as Ottawa has made and as Halifax can make.
I have one suggestion to offer, and it is this. Within a few weeks the dominion-provincial conference will meet in Ottawa to go into a number of matters affecting the relations between the provinces and the dominion. One matter which, I suggest, could very well be considered at that conference is this question of the right of municipalities to tax the property of the crown. The position of cities and municipalities throughout the dominion should not be prejudiced for all time merely by reason of the fact that in 1867 our constitution provided that property of Canada was not taxable.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP PAYMENT OF $300,000 FOR FIVE YEARS ENDING JULY 1, 1949
speechtext:
I rise to support the motion. I fully appreciate the disabilities suffered by municipalities in which the government have large and substantial holdings. When I had the privilege of serving on the confederation of mayors this subject became quite an old chestnut. One of the principal complainants was the city of Niagara Falls, where Ontario hydro has a huge installation. I agree that this grant is indeed due
to the city of Ottawa, but the observation I particularly wish to make is that I think there should be some practical yardstick or scientific formula applied1 in such matters. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Boucher) has made reference to the amount of taxes which would have been received by the city of Ottawa had the government been subject to the same rate of taxation in relation to their assessed properties as are private individuals. One can appreciate that this proposed payment is, as it were, a mere contribution. The time is not far distant when we should determine by some formula the amount or percentage of amounts that the dominion and provincial governments should pay, either in taxation or in substitution for the taxes they would otherwise be expected to pay. I do not think it should be a matter of a grant which is meant in a sense to compensate for services rendered by the city of Ottawa. Surely this great country with its resources can afford to pay its way. While accepting the resolution, I suggest that in our future approach to the matter we should find some method of determining the .amount of taxes which dominion property should return to the municipality for the services which are rendered by the municipality, without resorting to what is more or less a guess of $300,000 in the light of the figures presented by the hon. member for Carleton. I hope that in the not too distant future we shall determine that it will not be $300,000 but a reasonable amount in relation to what we pay for services that are rendered by the capital city to the nation as a whole.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP PAYMENT OF $300,000 FOR FIVE YEARS ENDING JULY 1, 1949
speechtext:
As a member of the committee, I have one word to say. I would ask the minister to explain in committee how far the government has gone in implementing the other recommendations. While I realize that from the Ottawa council's point of view $300,000' is a great increase over the $100,000 previously granted, there are other recommendations in which as a member of the committee I am greatly interested. We are coming now into the period of snow. There is a recommendation with regard to the clearing of snow from the streets of Ottawa and the collection of ashes and garbage. The suggestion from the committee was that this be done on a cooperative basis. Regarding the street transportation system, has anything been done there? And as regards the city as a national capital, it has been recommended that other sections of Canada be given representation on the commission. I think it is due the house, especially after the time taken up by the committee last year, that a statement be made by the
City of Ottawa Agreement

minister with reference to these various recommendations. When may we expect the implementing of them?

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP PAYMENT OF $300,000 FOR FIVE YEARS ENDING JULY 1, 1949
speechtext:
The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) referred to the federal district commission, but that is a matter which does not come within this resolution. The federal district commission comes under another department, and when the estimates for the federal district commission come before the house for consideration that will be the proper time to discuss the other recommendations of the committee that sat in 1944. This bill has special purposes which are embodied in the agreement, and one provision is the increasing of the payment for services rendered by the city from $100,000 to $300,000. That amount was arrived at after evidence had been heard in the committee. We thought there would be more satisfaction to the public if witnesses appeared and presented the city's case to both houses. In our opinion that was preferable to having an arbitrary figure decided upon by the government. We are adopting this unanimous recommendation from that committee.
As regards presenting the report of that committee for discussion, I do not believe, from my past experience in the house, that concurrence can be asked1 for in a succeeding session or a succeeding parliament. I am no expert in these matters of procedure but I do not believe that can be done. As I have said, however, when the estimates for the federal district commission come up the recommendations can be discussed.
There are only four recommendations. One has to do with the extension of the territory surrounding the capital, and the extension of the powers and the number of commissioners on the federal district commission, There is also the recommendation regarding the power to set up committees to negotiate with municipalities concerning future works that may be carried out. One recommendation had to do with the displacing of the union station, and another recommendation concerns the cleanliness of the city, the removal of snow from streets and parks, and the collection of ashes, garbage and other refuse. Under this bill, with the little knowledge I have of the situation, I could discuss the report, but when the bill is distributed to members they will see the scope of the agreement, and at that time I can answer questions.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Golding in the chair.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP PAYMENT OF $300,000 FOR FIVE YEARS ENDING JULY 1, 1949
speechtext:
In my opinion we are not
justified in making fish of one community in the dominion and fowl of another. We have

been told this afternoon that this payment, by which it is proposed to increase from $100,000 to $300,000 the grant to the city of Ottawa is for services rendered by the city to the dominion government. But I would ask, what about the services that have: been rendered by the dominion government to the city of Ottawa? The dominion government has established in the city of Ottawa one of the biggest industries that exist in this country, namely the parliament of Canada; and if the city of Ottawa objects in any way to having that industry continued here, under the terms on which it was established, I can assure the citizens of this city and the members of this house that there are a great many communities in the dominion that would be very glad to take over the industry which the dominion has established. They will give it a free site; they will give it free water; they will give it free police and fire protection, and they will let it set up their plant there without any taxation whatsoever.
If the dominion government is to give compensation to Ottawa in lieu of permitting it to tax dominion properties in this city, then I think they will have to treat other cities in Canada in the same way. As has been said here this afternoon, the British North America Act provides that dominion property shall be free of taxation. If the government is to change that principle it cannot do so for one city alone. The act should be amended and the government should be fair to the other cities in the dominion. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I want to say that I am opposed to the agreement.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP PAYMENT OF $300,000 FOR FIVE YEARS ENDING JULY 1, 1949
speechtext:
The city of Toronto has in its tax rate to-day about two and a half or two and three-quarter mills on the dollar which are purely federal. That tax rate is imposed on real estate in our city because the dominion government pays no taxes in that city. This agreement calls for the payment of $300,000 to Ottawa. That will amount to a cash grant of $1,500,000 in five years. That money will be handed to the city of Ottawa for what? As a subvention in exchange for municipal services rendered. But to that must be added the capital expenditures which have been undertaken by the federal district commission and the suburban roads commission. Roads, squares, parks and driveways in this city have been built at federal expense. In every other municipality these things are paid for by the taxpayers of the municipality. This is quite unfair and it is getting everything out of joint. The other municipalities make their complaints to the government year after year, but they

City of Ottawa Agreement
receive nothing. Nevertheless the municipalities have spent money on the very same kind of services. I pointed out the difference in the United States and in Great Britain. In Great Britain they have a regulation through the local government board by which in effect they pay the cost of these very services. The government of this country is not doing so. If the government wants to ruin real estate by such federal burdens imposed on it, all very well. The time has come for a halt until we have more equality of treatment for other places.
The government has erected a large number of buildings in this city. I speak from memory, but I believe that during the war ten million or eleven million dollars worth of buildings have been put up and all that sort of thing. We have to consider the way in which this reacts on the taxpayers of the country. This money comes out of revenue, out of income. This $300,000 which is payable to the city of Ottawa is in the federal tax rate and directly charged to income. I suggest that some consideration should be given to the other municipalities. I join in the complaints of the junior hon. member for Halifax, the hon. member for New Westminster and other hon. members along the same line.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP PAYMENT OF $300,000 FOR FIVE YEARS ENDING JULY 1, 1949
speechtext:
I do not wish to see this opportunity go by without saying a word about one of the municipalities in which I am interested, namely the municipality of Esquimalt. I am not opposing the bill or the granting of $300,000 to Ottawa. I am inclined to agree with the junior hon. member for Halifax that this gives us some reason to hope that the government will look farther than Ottawa at some of the other municipalities which are not being treated quite fairly. Fifty-five per cent of the municipality of Esquimalt is owned by the dominion government. I agree that it is a small municipality. Year after year we have been asking for the small sum of $10,000 a year to maintain the roads and sidewalks that are used almost exclusively for military purposes, but we have not been able to get any recognition whatever. I suppose it is quite all right to say that under the British North America Act municipalities are not allowed to tax crown property, but we have come quite a piece since that time, and I think the whole matter of taxation of crown property should be reconsidered.
Esquimalt is a naval base, and also a base for the military district which gives service to all of Canada, and not to the municipality of Esquimalt alone; therefore I think it should be given some financial assistance to take care
of the upkeep of the roads and the services that go with them. If it is a matter of a post office or a customs office, these are things that give service to the community and the property should not be taxed; but where it is a matter of service to the whole of Canada then, in my opinion, some allowances should be made the community for it. I wish to say I do not want to see this bill go by default. I am putting up a plea for some recognition for the small municipalities that find themselves in a very difficult position at the present time.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP PAYMENT OF $300,000 FOR FIVE YEARS ENDING JULY 1, 1949
speechtext: In order to show that this request from the municipality of Esquimalt is quite removed from party politics I should like to add my support to the remarks which have just been made by the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.), because the municipality of Esquimalt is partly in the federal district of Nanaimo, and I can vouch for every word that he has uttered as to the very heavy burden which that small municipality has carried. In addition to that, I would add that the rural country just behind that municipality has also had to bear a heavy burden for the maintenance of their roads which have been severely damaged by the heavy military traffic, for which they were never designed, in moving from the Esquimalt naval dock and the central forts into the outlying forts in the district. If this is an indication that the present government intends to help those municipalities which are bearing a heavy burden from the dominion point of view, then I would certainly approve the idea of assisting Ottawa in that respect; but as has already been said, this policy must apply not only to Ottawa; it should apply to all those other places where a heavy federal burden is borne by a small municipality.

Equality of treatment is
all we ask for.

It strikes me
that the situation of Ottawa is not quite the same as that of other cities throughout the country.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OP PAYMENT OF $300,000 FOR FIVE YEARS ENDING JULY 1, 1949
speechtext:
In 1858 Ottawa
was just one of those very small towns. It was chosen as the capital of the country. After confederation buildings went up and we had to apply to this town for services, to use their waterworks services. That is the way it started. In 1877 we signed an agreement to pay them $7,000 a year. If you look around to the other cities in the country which were built independently of government functions, and where the people are asking the government every day to put up public buildings,
City oj Ottawa Agreement

you will see that the situation, is different. That does not occur in Ottawa. I do not want to defend Ottawa too much; I happen to live across the river. I sympathize with all these members who are asking for recognition for their towns and cities. I happen to live in a town just across from the capital city of Ottawa. There is no grant given to that town, though they have public buildings there.
Really the principle is not new. If we are not to change section 125 of the British North America Act, which provides that no land or property belonging to the federal or provincial governments is liable to taxation, I do not know how in this capital city we can get the services we need without paying those who have the facilities. That is the way I see it. I do not believe the amount of $300,000 is actually too much, in view of all the new construction that has been put up during the war, which certainly was not requested by anyone in the city of Ottawa. I think it is only fair that we should pay for the fire protection, water service, police protection and so on.

subtopic: DEFINITION OF FISH TO INCLUDE SHELLFISHPROCESSING AND MARKING-POWER OF SEIZURE AND CONFISCATION

speechtext: Hon. H. F. G. BRIDGES (Minister of Fisheries) moved the second reading of bill No. 91, to amend the Fish Inspection Act.

subtopic: DEFINITION OF FISH TO INCLUDE SHELLFISHPROCESSING AND MARKING-POWER OF SEIZURE AND CONFISCATION
speechtext: Would the minister be good enough to make a statement on the bill.

subtopic: DEFINITION OF FISH TO INCLUDE SHELLFISHPROCESSING AND MARKING-POWER OF SEIZURE AND CONFISCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this bill was introduced into the house I stated that the objects of the same were threefold: first, to extend the definition of the word "fish" to include shellfish. Possibly it would have been wiser on my part if I had used the word "clarify". The real object is to clarify the definition of the word "fish" to include shellfish. The second object is to enable the governor in council to make regulations respecting the processing and marking of fish to be packed in containers. The third object is to provide for seizure as well as for powers of confiscation upon conviction for an offence against the act or regulations. The last named addition will bring this act in line with the Fisheries Act and the Meat and Canned Foods Act.	.
I do not know that there is any necessity for me to elaborate any further at this stage. We are all most anxious to have the business of the house expedited as quickly as possible. In moving the second reading of this bill I should' like to point out that after second reading takes place it is my intention to move that the bill be referred to the standing committee on marine and fisheries. I feel, and I am sure most hon. members will agree with me, that a bill of this kind is a most, appropriate one to be referred to one of our standing committees. I believe that most of the members of this house who are interested in the fishing industry are members of that standing committee. Therefore there will be ample opportunity for a full'discussion of the bill and its merits before that standing committee. I do not think there is any need for me to say anything further at this time.

subtopic: DEFINITION OF FISH TO INCLUDE SHELLFISHPROCESSING AND MARKING-POWER OF SEIZURE AND CONFISCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just one word to say. First, may I compliment the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Bridges) upon his intention to refer this bill to the marine and fisheries committee. It is some seven or eight years since this committee has had anything referred to it. I should like to suggest that in the session to follow he refer to that committee the Fisheries Act. If there is any act on the statute books that needs overhauling, it is our Fisheries Act. Since this bill has just three sections I think we can easily deal with it during the present session.

Fish Inspection Act

subtopic: DEFINITION OF FISH TO INCLUDE SHELLFISHPROCESSING AND MARKING-POWER OF SEIZURE AND CONFISCATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I agree that the proper procedure in regard to this bill is to refer it to the marine and fisheries committee. I understand that at the moment this is not a bill of wide implications, and the committee will be in better position to deal with it than we in the house. I agree that this is the proper procedure.

subtopic: DEFINITION OF FISH TO INCLUDE SHELLFISHPROCESSING AND MARKING-POWER OF SEIZURE AND CONFISCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the speaker who preceded me that this bill can very well be referred to the marine and fisheries committee, but before it is so referred, there are one or two questions I should like to ask the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Bridges). The bill states that the underlined words are added to remove any doubts as to the inclusion of shellfish under the act. I wish to ask the minister when any doubt first arose that shellfish were not included under the very wide definition of "fish" contained in the act. When did a question come to the attention of his department that caused any doubts to the meaning of this word in the act, as a result of which this amendment is now proposed?
Any doubt that arose must have come up after May 13, 1932, which is the date of chapter 31 of the statutes of that year which amended the act and provided that the governor in council had the right to make regulations concerning oysters. Evidently it was thought at that time that shellfish came under the act, for if that had not been the case the amendment would not have been made in 1932.
The bill grants additional powers to make regulations. The Fish Inspection Act, which is chapter 72 of the Revised Statutes of 1927, states in section 4, subsection 2:
All regulations made hereunder shall take effect from the date mentioned therein for the purpose, and shall be published in the Canada Gazette and in the prefix in the volume of the statutes of Canada published next after the making thereof.
It is amazing to find that the provisions in other acts with respect to the publication of regulations vary considerably. I shall not take up the time of the house in reading those particular sections about regulations in a number of other acts, but I would point out that the Live Stock and Live Stock Products Act, which is chapter 120 of the Revised Statutes of 1927, contains a different provision. The Importation and Sales Act, chapter 100, Revised Statutes of 1927, contains another provision and the Meats and Canned Foods Act contains another provision about regulations. You can pick out other acts and you will find that this section regarding publication
of regulations is worded in a different way. I think the time has come when a committee of the house should be set up to consider the question of regulations and government by order in council. I believe that we have been drafting these sections in the different acts for a long enough time now to adopt some standard form to be inserted in acts with regard to the publication of regulations.
May I add this? Under our form of democratic government the people who elected us to the House of Commons elected us to make the laws. The Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Ilsley) the other day used words to that effect when he addressed this house; and we are neglecting our duty as members of this house when we allow the laws to be made by order in council. So far as regulations dealing purely with administrative matters are concerned, it seems to me that there is no objection to their being made by order in council on recommendation of the minister; but when it comes to regulations that have the force of law and impose a penalty, then the members of this house are neglecting their duty in permitting that to be done, for we were elected to make the laws and we have no right to delegate that authority.
Another question that I would ask the minister is this. What is the difference between a fishery inspector and a fishery guardian? Are they both appointed by the civil service commission, or has the minister or his department the power to appoint one of these officials, the other being appointed by the civil service commission? I ask this question because I was informed recently that a fishery inspector living near Shediac, New Brunswick, resigned early this year to take another position. A resident of the community wrote the Department of Fisheries on behalf of a soldier who had returned from overseas after nearly six years of service, had been wounded at Cannes and was a married man with two children. In reply the writer of the letter was informed that the position was not open yet but that when it was open it would be advertised by the civil service commission and that the qualifications were that the applicant had to have a high-school education and a knowledge of the fishing business. The position was not, I am informed, advertised by the civil service commission, but was filled by the Department of Fisheries by the appointment of a man who never had a high-school education, knew little about the fishing business and had never served overseas although he was in the ground forces of the R.C.A.F. for a time. It seems to me that we are entitled to some explanation of this appointment.
Fish Inspection Act

speechtext:
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of bill No. 92, to amend the Penitentiary Act, 1939.
He said:	When the bill was introduced and
read the first time I made a brief statement as to its object, and I do not know that at this time there is anything that I should add. Hon. members know that the penitentiaries royal commission had recommended the appointment of a commission of three persons to administer the penitentiaries and had also made a large number of other recommendations for the improvement of the penal institutions in Canada, many of which would necessitate agreement with the provincial authorities and probably some constitutional amendment. Following the report in 1939, an

Penitentiary Act
act was adopted to provide for its implementing, but the act was to come into force only on proclamation. Before proclamation was issued war broke out, and it was felt that during the period of the war it would not be proper to go on with the projects recommended by the commission. Active hostilities have tow ceased, and there is hope that within a reasonable time both the shortage of materials which will be required for the additional construction necessary to carry out recommendations of the report, and the shortage of man-power for additional trained staff that will also be necessary, may have ceased and that it will be possible to do something which a great many consider is long overdue toward the amelioration of our penal institutions, especially in the aspect of reform for those confined in those institutions.
The act as adopted in 1939 would require, if it were to be (proclaimed, at least one amendment. There was a provision in the act that the appropriations made for the penitentiaries branch of the Department of Justice would be available during the fiscal year 1939-40 for the purposes of the new regime to be instituted under the statute. In order to proclaim the act at this time and to have it practicable there must be at least an amendment to that provision to make the appropriations voted for the fiscal year in which the act will be proclaimed available for use by the new body.
It is suggested that there be other slight amendments of the act. I am informed by the officers of the department that one of the difficulties my predecessor was up against in trying to form a commission was the fact that the act provided for the appointment of commissioners for a period of ten years without any provision being made for superannuation or retirement pension, and that it was not attractive for the kind of men who would be apt to be proper officials to carry out the important functions provided for. It is therefore being suggested that the commissioners be appointed during pleasure and that they come under the Superannuation Act.
A second suggestion is that, instead of having to appoint at once three commissioners, the governor in council may appoint one or more commissioners; and my intention is, when the act or that part of it which would apply is proclaimed, to try to find one who would be a competent chairman of the commission and to have him do the preliminary work-because there is a lot to be done before the new system can be fully operated- and make concrete recommendations which can be brought to parliament in the estimates for implementing.
One of the features about which the most concern has been expressed is that which would have to do with the establishment in Canada of something similar to the Borstal system in the United Kingdom. The commission in making its report stated emphatically that the Borstal system could not be established in the penitentiaries, that it is something which would have to be a corollary of a unified system of penal institutions in and for Canada. If I had nothing else to attend to and could devote my whole time to the preparation of what is required to implement the penitentiary report it might not be necessary to delegate the preliminary work to someone else, but my experience is that I shall not and that none of the present officers of the Department of Justice will have the time to do that, and that if it is to be done-and I do not see how anything practicable can be worked out without its being done-we shall have to get a good full-time man to take this report, investigate the situation of each one of the penitentiaries, interview the provincial departments in each one of the provinces, and see to what extent it will be possible to get some agreement on some unified system of administering the penal institutions of the country.
It may be necessary for the appointee, before proceeding very far along these lines, personally to go and make some studies of the systems in the United Kingdom and in some of the states of the United States of America and recommend then the details of the changes to be made in order that we may have a system of penal institutions that will be more helpful in the task of reforming many of those who are sentenced to gaol or given penitentiary sentences. As a matter of fact, the situation is not too bad here. I suppose there is not an hon. member who does not know of some one or more cases where laudable reform has taken place in the conduct and manner of living of some poor unfortunate who had fallen by the wayside. But unfortunately that is not the general rule, and there is considerable room for at least the hope of improvement by providing additional assistance to some of those unfortunate persons who do succumb. The purpose of this bill is to make as speedily as it can be made the preparation and implementing of concrete proposals to that end. The bill is noit a long one. The statute itself had fully covered the ground and the only substantial changes are the three I have mentioned.

subtopic: TERM OF OFFICE OF COMMISSIONERS-SUPERANNUATION-PROCLAMATION OF ACT IN PART OR WHOLE
speechtext:
I am sure that those of us who have familiarized ourselves with the causes of the background that sends young men or women or old men
Penitentiary Act

to the penitentiary, those of us who have familiarized ourselves, through our dealings with others, with what goes on in the penitentiaries, and those of us who know something of the fight that those who have come out and want to make good have had to put up in meeting the difficulties against which they have to struggle, will welcome the amendment, especially in the second clause providing for the appointment of a commissioner to study the commendable proposals that were made by the royal commission.
I have congratulated' the Minister of Justice on former occasions on the fact that he did not wish to have men complete sentences in the penitentiary if this could be avoided, but was willing to let a man out when he showed a desire to be a decent citizen. He allowed me to have two men out during last summer, and they have conducted themselves so well since they came out that they would compare favourably with the members of this house in their conduct. I would say too that out of the 130 that I have had an opportunity of sponsoring there has been only one man who has gone back to Burwash. The reason for his return there is that he was too fond of something that injured his power of thinking, and he would not turn to that permanent cure for alcohol or any other evil which to me is the only cure for sin or anything else.
I commend the minister for his humanity in being willing to put into practice the findings of the royal commission, because I know well the character of one of the men on that commission, a former attorney general of Manitoba, a clear-thinking graduate of old Manitoba university. These men can conduct themselves on any commission with credit, and I am proud to think that the minister is now preparing to put into practice the findings of that royal commission. I am sure we shall all give him wholehearted support.
Mr. JOHN T. HACKETT (Stanstead): This is another piece of legislation which is without any partisan appeal. To borrow an adjective from the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat, it is a humanitarian piece of legislation and it will have, I am sure, the support and best consideration of the house. I regret, however, that further delay seems to be anticipated in giving effect to the findings of the commission.
It will very shortly be ten years since this commission was named.. I know that the Minister of Justice was not responsible for the relays resulting from the great war. This -bill is not a very long one, and the responsibility of the minister may not go beyond it. But I must tell him that it is thoroughly disap-
[Mr. Mclvor.3
pointing to the house to learn that the putting into effect of legislation as important as that, of 1939 should be further delayed by an investigation into the findings of the royal commission.
Royal commissions on penal reform have been numerous in this country. In 1832 a commission was appointed by the legislature of Upper Canada and there have been a great many such investigations since. Between 1911 and 1914 I had a good deal to do with the administration of the penitentiaries. While in Europe in 1912, I visited a number of penal institutions in England and a number in France. Shortly after that a commission was named primarily to investigate and report upon conditions at Kingston. But the inquiries and recommendations of that commission did extend to the penal system of all Canada. A little later, in 1920, another commission was appointed and finally the Areham-bault commission was set-up. They all came to the same end: nothing was done. The Archambault commission investigated for about two years. Its members spent a number of months in foreign countries, and they brought in a complete and detailed report. That commission advised that a penitentiary commission be set up. The legislation was enacted by parliament in the month of April, 1939. Once the war began it was probably proper to wait until it was over before implementing the legislation, but there was no very good reason between the month of April, 1939, and the month of September for doing nothing about the matter The bill has been twice amended and we now have to consider another amendment.
The purpose of this bill according to one of the first sections is, as the minister has stated, to inquire into the report of the Archambault commission and tell the government what portion of it should be put into force. I regret these dilatory methods. The matter is one of utmost urgency. I am aware and the house is aware that the minister himself cannot be expected to engage in detail of that kind, but the fact is that a commission of extremely able men spent two years in investigating and putting into perfect form and into a concise series of recommendations the result of their labours. With great- deference. I suggest that it seems a waste of time to investigate further the findings of the commission.
Without this legislation some person should be found who could advise the minister as he is advised daily in the many aspects of the work of his department, and thus enable him to give immediate effect to this much-needed legislation. What is more disturbing

Penitentiary Act
is that the minister says that if effect is to be given1 to all the recommendations, some constitutional amendments will have to be made. Well, Mr. Speaker, if any measure of penal reform must remain in abeyance until the tangled skein of dominion-provincial relations is untangled, then we must abandon all hope of reforming in our time our penal system. It is true that the provinces have jurisdiction over their gaols. The sooner we set them the good example of reforming our penitentiaries, the sooner will reform permeate the whole Canadian system.
What is to be said for further delay? The war is over. People are ready and willing to consider all manner of social reform. When one travels abroad and sees something of the penal systems of other countries one realizes how much it is possible to do for those unfortunate Canadians who by some accident, of birth or training, are spending weary days behind the bars.
I venture to submit to the house that there will be no legislation brought forward at this session that has greater possibilities of frustration than this. People who have been looking forward for a chance to mend their ways and youth which needs the benefit of these reforms are going to be disappointed if all further reform is to await further investigation. I suggest to the minister that he find someone-and he need not go very far or take much time in finding someone-who would be able to present to him in succinct form the kernel of the findings of the Archambault commission. He suggests that it may be necessary to go to the United States and to England. That is exactly what the Archambault commissioners did. They went to the United States; they went to England, to France, to Belgium, to Holland; they went to all countries which have a penal system worthy of study. They made a complete investigation and they informed the government what should be done. Surely, when the government set up the penitentiary commission in 1939 they did not anticipate that it would be necessary to set up another commission to find out what the first commission meant when it made its report. For these reasons I submit to the house it is unfortunate that there should be further delay in implementing that part of the Archambault report which has the approval of the government.

speechtext:
For
a great many years this matter has been coming before the House of Commons in the estimates in the last days of the session. It has been discussed on the estimates of the minister's department,. We have been twentyfive years behind the times in the administration of this department. When I first came to the bouse I pointed out that the city of Toronto- h-ad spent a large sum of money in establishing a farm on north Yonge street and another women's farm. Deputations have appeared before the government asking for reforms. They got it in England twenty-five or thirty years ago in the Borstal system. What do we find here? We are away behind the times. Members of parliament do not have to get a permit from the minister to visit the penitentiaries; under the act they are classed as visitors. I brought a bill into this house in 1924 or 1925 and on different occasions to allow grand juries to visit these institutions twice a year in the cities or towns in which federal prisons are located and to present a report to the minister. I remember a charge to a grand jury at the Toronto fall assizes in 1927 by the late Chief Justice R. M. Meredith, one of the most prominent trial judges this country ever had, who stated that since magna charta it was a cardinal principle that the people should have a large share in the administration of justice, and that grand juries should be allowed to go into these various penal institutions, both federal and provincial, in county towns throughout Canada. I should be glad if I could have not only the attention of the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) while I -am dealing with these matters, but that of the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent), who is also the Attorney General. The chief justice said that, whether rightly or wrongly, these institutions were managed by crown officers; and it was one of the principles of magna charta that no one should be imprisoned without a trial by his peers. A grand jury had found a sane man in an asylum. For many years the chief justice urged on departments this question of a rigid system of inspection, and I am sorry the government of the, day has not adopted that principle.
The result is that these institutions are inspected only by crown officers. The visitors' books show that hardly anyone else visits them; yet they are an agency of this parliament, and we are supposed to be living in a civilized country. After all is said and done, Christianity is part of the law of England and automatically became part of the law of Canada by the Constitutional Act of 1792. We find grand juries all over the country bringing in reports with regard to very poor conditions in provincial, municipal and federal prisons. There has been a great deal of talk of prison reform in the Christian churches, as well as in the Jewish churches. In Toronto we have a civic institution in my constituency,
Penitentiary Act

walls around it and no one can get in. The grand jury cannot go in there, only officials once in a while from Ottawa, and yet it is kept up with the taxpayers' money. It was the armed strength of the barons that gave us the magna charta. As one of the great administrators of criminal law has said, these institutions are managed, whether rightly or wrongly, by crown officers. Many of these men had no previous experience in this work. They learn something about human nature by experience only or being called upon to act in a minor capacity at one of their institutions. It may be that they are appointed by patronage or by members of parliament. I do not charge this government with that any more than any other government, but that has been the practice in these institutions from time immemorial.
I complained to the splendid and efficient officer commanding No. 3 district, and he wrote me a letter which I shall not read. Many of these men were moved from Fort Henry into those two other institutions. I contend that under the act the wardens had no right to receive them; they had no authority under the laws of the province or the Penitentiary Act of Canada. If the wardens did receive them they were liable for civil damages for illegal detention.
I ask for some reforms. Mr. Justice Mackay of Toronto as one of the finest trial judges in Canada. He was the able judge in a libel suit between the Toronto Globe and Mail and the Toronto Star which lasted for some days. If we had a new royal commission made up of men like him we might get somewhere on this reform. The minister now has an assistant known as the Solicitor General to get speedier results, whom I do not see here to-night. If this matter is handled like the internments I venture to say it will be months and months before anything is done, and few will get out of the trenches by Christmas.
I am glad that the minister has decided to carry out some of the principles of the report of the commission and I wish him every success in his work. He has been a zealous and faithful, hard-working Attorney-General and I hope, being the humanitarian he is, he will try to get some value for the money. The taxpayers of Canada expect reforms in this department and want value for their money.
I complained also about the provincial and municipal institutions. They are all relics, some of the middle ages. Some of these institutions were built before confederation. Many of them have been condemned as being unfit for civilians. If they are, why are they considered good enough in some cases for soldiers, especially soldiers who for two or three years 
were good soldiers? These men have had their gratuities and other credits as well taken away and their suffering wives and children are out on the street. I hope the minister will get something done. I hope he will do it now. It would be a good thing if each minister had on his desk a sign, "Do it now."

subtopic: TERM OF OFFICE OF COMMISSIONERS-SUPERANNUATION-PROCLAMATION OF ACT IN PART OR WHOLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I first read this amendment to the Penitentiary Act the same thing struck me as struck the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor), namely, that the commissioners were to be appointed to consider the report of the royal commission to investigate the penal system of Canada. This is a step in the right direction. It is a small step, but a step just the same. I endorse the view that has been put forward by the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett), because I believe that the government could have gone much farther in this penal reform. I wish to endorse everything that has been said by the hon. member for Fort William and the hon. member for Stanstead in praise of Mr. Justice Archambault and his associates on the commission. They did some wonderful work. I do not think I ever read a report of a royal commission that exhibited more painstaking work and more courage in their recommendations.
In 1939, subsequently to that report being received, a new Penitentiary Act was passed which, however, has not yet come into force. I have studied this new act and compared it with the old law clause by clause, and I can see no fundamental change with the exception that a commission is to be appointed instead of a superintendent. No doubt some of the appalling conditions disclosed in the report have been rectified, but these conditions were due to inefficient and incompetent personnel. The new act proposes no fundamental changes and unless the government or those charged with the administration of our penitentiaries are vigilant some of the conditions disclosed in that report may return. However, what interested me particularly in the report was not so much the sensational disclosures of the acts and omissions of inefficient officials as the underlying fundamental complaint of the commission that our penitentiary system is more a system of punishment than a system of paying attention to the reformation of the convict, and there is the further startling fact that our present system makes real habitual criminals out of those who could be reformed and made useful members of society. That startling fact is as true to-day as it was at the time the commission made its report.
Our prison population is still increasing, and while there has been some reduction in the

Penitentiary Act
number of convictions during the1 last few years of the war, to which reduction I shall refer later, the number of recidivists, that is repeaters, has alarmingly increased. According to a statistical table on page 214 of the commission's report, supplemented by figures which I find on page 983 of the last Canada Year Book, conditions in our country are really appalling. In 1931 the recidivists, offenders who have more than two convictions against them, totalled 3,047; in 1939 they totalled 18,232; in 1942 second offenders totalled over 13,097. There was some decrease in 1942, and of course I claim that it is due to the war and the consequent period of employment and relative prosperity. I shall refer to that later.
I have _ not the figures for recidivists or plural offenders for England and Wales, but the report contains the total number of convictions in the mother country between 1931 and 1936, and a comparison of the figures for England and Wales with the figures for Canada speaks volumes. In 1931, 46,810 convictions for indictable offenses in England and Wales compare with 31,542 in Canada. In 1933 the number of convictions in England and Wales was 42,248 as compared with 32,942 in Canada. In 1935 the number of convictions in England and Wales was 47,424 as compared with 33,531 in Canada, or, roughly, 118 per 100,000 of population of England and Wales as against 305 per 100,000 of population in Canada. The latest Canadian figure, for 1942, is 337 per 100,000 of population in Canada. Commenting on the state of affairs, the commissioners say:
The above figures cast a grave reflection on the methods of treating convicted prisoners in Canada. That the number convicted three times or more per 1,000 of convicted persons, should have risen from 87 in 1922 to 224 in 1936 indicates that the present system is neither effecting reformation nor affording protection to society against further offences by prisoners when liberated.
The commission makes detailed and specific recommendations as to how we should cope with this situation; that is, with the reformation of prisoners. I shall first refer to their recommendations for prisoners in general and later to their recommendations as to the treatment of young offenders. Roughly, their recommendations are as follows: (a) segregation; (b) the grades and merit system; (c) proper medical treatment and analysis; (d) a programme of recreation and reading; (e) education; (f) centralization and unification of our prison system.
Time will not permit me to go into detail with respect to these recommendations, but
just a word about segregation, or rather the absence of segregation. This is what the commission say in their report:
It is hopeless to strive to effect the reformation of a prisoner while, at the same time, exposing him to the destructive association of depraved criminals who have no determination to live anything but degenerate lives of crime.
. . . The undeniable responsibility of the state to those held in its custody is to see that they are not returned to freedom worse than when they were taken in charge.
No attempt is made at segregation; in fact, because of our system no attempt can be made at segregation. We have seven penitentiaries throughout Canada, and prisoners are sent to the penitentiary nearest to the locality in which they were convicted. Therefore we could only make an attempt at segregation if we could send prisoners to a particular penitentiary set aside for a particular class of convicts, and there is no such arrangement.
In company with four colleagues I visited Kingston penitentiary a few weeks ago and as the law and regulations now stand, so far as the taking care of the physical welfare of the prisoners is concerned we found conditions in that institution as good as could be expected. I believe that the officers with whom I came in contact are interested in their duties, and by the way I might mention that considering the responsibilities which some of them carry, I think they are woefully underpaid. There is no segregation at Kingston, and of course there cannot be any. Some of the prisoners as we walked through the corridors were through with their work and were conversing freely with each other. There was no segregation, and young prisoners undoubtedly were mixing with old, seasoned criminals. You could not have a different work-shop for each different co'nvict, for there is not sufficient room.
They have a classroom in Kingston, and now for a few minutes I am going to speak about education. They have also a teacher in that institution, although we did not have an opportunity of talking with him because it was Saturday afternoon and he was not on duty. There was no compulsion to attend classes except that illiterates are compelled to learn to read and write; also those who have not reached either grade 3 or grade 4 are forced to attend classes. We went through one cell block and were invited to go into the cells because the prisoners were out at their work at that particular time. There is a little table in each cell and above it a shelf where they keep books and other personal effects. The cells I inspected, about ten of them, showed that each of the inmates took some interest in reading. I took the trouble
Penitentiary Act

of looking to see what books they were interested in, and I am sorry to say that all these books were fiction, and pulp paper magazines at that. There was only one prisoner who seemed to be interested in somewhat different reading. I found that he had an English-French dictionary and a French high school grammer such as would be used in an Englishspeaking high school. I find that no real progress has been made with respect to education since the commission made its report. Let me quote from the report of the commission with regard to this question of the schooling of prisoners and the regulations pertaining to education-page 114:
The observance of these regulations is largely perfunctory, and individual examination and schooling of the prisoners is almost entirely lacking. The teacher, himself, is not given the recognition to which the importance of his work entitles him. Even his uniform as an officer is of a lower grade than that of the other members of the staff who form the classification board. This inferiority of status not only reacts upon the teachers themselves, but has a tendency to lessen their Standing in the eyes of the prison population.
The commission goes on to comment upon the low salaries paid to teachers, and states -page 119:
Teachers and librarians who are selected should have training in pedagogy and in librarianship, and have the necessary personality and zeal to carry out the important task these officers are called upon to perform. . . .
When suitable and1 properly trained teachers ana librarians are secured, they should be paid an adequate remuneration and given an adequate status in the official personnel;
Even for the coming year there seems to be no prospect of making any progress, because the penitentiary estimates provide for no increase in teachers. The estimates provide for five teachers and one assistant teacher for seven penitentiaries, so that some penitentiaries must go without. A teacher is paid $1,860 and the assistant is paid $1,800. Can we say that $1,860 is adequate for a man who should be competent to teach almost anything, even university subjects? That is not as ridiculous as it may sound. The officer who guided us through the penitentiary told us of some young man who took up his high school course in Kingston and then got two scholarships at Queen's university.
I would suggest that in connection with the training of teachers for our penitentiaries, training such as is suggested in the royal commission's report, we should set up one or two training schools at our universities or other institutions of learning and provide scholarships to the right men, available to some of the officers who are now on duty in our penitentiaries, in order that we might produce for our penitentiaries a teaching staff which

is not only fitted academically but also trained to deal with the particular pupils who may be in their charge.
The last report of the acting superintendent makes mention of some steps being taken to give some of our officers courses in job training. I understand that over one hundred of these officers have taken advantage of this course. While this is a good start, it is in my opinion entirely inadequate. The course consists of five iectures of two hours each, or a total of ten hours, after which the officer gets a certain certificate, and that is as far as they go. There is no question in my mind that the trade instructors whom we have in our penitentiaries should be classified as teachers, in a way. They are the superintendents at the different workshops attached to our penal institutions. I was very much impressed with the trade shops and also with the trade instructors in them. These trade instructors are doing a really fine job. In Kingston they have a mailbag workshop, a printing shop, a shoe factory, a machine shop, a garage, a paint shop, et cetera. The prisoners who work in those shops are paid five cents a day, and as I said, the trade instructor supervises the work in each of these departments. The instructors with whom I talked all take a keen interest in their work and a great pride in the products of their respective shops. I was particularly interested in the printing shop, where they do very fine work indeed with some obsolete machinery. I would suggest to the minister that they get a linotype machine in Kingston, and if they have that, I can assure hon. members that they can print anything in Kingston. At the present time they are printing all the forms and books, and they do the bookbinding for the penitentiaries themselves and also for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. It seems to me that we are short of printers in Ottawa at the present time, at least as regards government printing, and I would suggest-facetiously, of course-that some of this printing be done in Kingston, where they can do a really fine job.

On the point which I quoted a little while ago, the commission, considering the importance of physical and mental defects as far as the criminal tendency of the prisoners is concerned, recommends some considerable changes, and I do not think there is anything that stands in the way of their present application in full.
Another important recommendation which should receive the immediate attention of the government is the centralization of the whole penal system in Canada under one commission, to which the hon. member for Stanstead referred a little while ago, I am quite satisfied that many of our people do not even know about the condition of our penitentiaries and how they are governed. They do not know that there are only seven penitentiaries under ' federal jurisdiction and that we send to them only prisoners who receive sentences of two years or more, while convicted persons whose sentences are less than two years are sent to provincial, municipal or county gaols. Our people do not know that the majority of the convicts sentenced under federal law's are sent to prisons which are not under federal jurisdiction. Thus in 1942, 12,655 persons convicted of indictable offences under the federal criminal code -were sent to municipal, provincial or county prisons, while only 2,521 convicts were sent to penitentiaries.
In order that we may have some effective prison reform, all our prisons should be under one central authority. This is what the commission says in this regard:
There is no doubt in the minds of your commissioners that uniformity of administration and the application of scientific principles to such administration, if made applicable to all those who are incarcerated in penal institutions in the Dominion of Canada, would provide a better penal system and one to which the recommendations of your commissioners could be most fittingly applied. It is obvious, for example, that if different treatment than that recommended by your commissioners is given to the prisoners in provincial institutions . . . and the administration is not, supervised by the same authorities, the success of the system recommended by your commissioners W'ould be jeopardized, and the evils discerned in the antiquated treatment at present in existence would be permanently extended. The federal authorities would be handicapped in the proper treatment of those who come to federal institutions already stamped with the imprints of the multiple provincial institutions.
Every country in the world except the United States of America and Canada possesses a centralized penal system.	,
The commissioners go to some extent in a general way into conditions existing at gaols and1 reformatories under the provincial, county or municipal jurisdictions, and come to the conclusion that they are quite inadequate- and that is a mild term. -

In England and Wales, with a population of approximately 41,000,000, they have twenty-five local prisons, four prisons under the Penal Servitude Act, one prison for women under this' act, one training centre, one preventive detention prison and seven Borstal institutions, or a total of thirty-nine. In Canada, with a population of around 12,000,000, we have twenty-two adult reformatories, seven penitentiaries and 118 provincial, county or municipal gaols, or a total of 147.
Do these figures not speak of the crying need of centralization of our whole prison system? I suggest to the government that perhaps at the forthcoming dominion-provincial conference this subject might at least be tentatively discussed, so that in the not too distant future we may have one centralized prison system in Canada. However, the most important item of reform which we need in Canada is the establishment of proper institutions for the treatment of young offenders between the ages of sixteen and twenty-one years. In fact I would include offenders up to twenty-three years as they do in England. It is with this class of prisoners that we should make a start in reformation. They are still young enough that, under proper guidance, direction and education, they can be moulded into good citizens.
The increase of crime in Canada, as shown by the figures which I presented a little while ago, applies equally to young offenders. According to the superintendent's report-the same report which I quoted a little while ago-there was on March 31, 1944, a total of 442 convicts under twenty-one years of age ifi our penitentiaries, an increase of seventy-nine over the previous year. I should like hon. gentlemen to study this graph a little, and I am sure they will agree with me that it is startling.

I should like to repeat what has been said for the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett), that happily this is not a partisan matter and happily-and I should like to emphasize this-in making suggestions to the Minister of Justice we are addressing them to a man who has no responsibility for the sad past, history of this situation.
I should like to remind you, Mr. Speaker, of the report of some thirty years and more ago, still waiting to be implemented. I can remember something about it. A great deal of honest, humane work was put into it. I know the members of the Biggar commission appointed some twelve years later also were humane men. They made recommendations. To-night we have heard high praise of Mr. Justice Archambault, who headed this last commission; and I believe if the members of this house would take five minutes to read some of the things in this report they would ask the Minister of Justice to take back this bill and bring in a bill that we could look at.
I should like to say just one thing about criminology. I am not an expert in it, but I take it we all agree that whatever amount of punishment we desire should be administered to people who fell by the way, we do not regard that as the whole job of penal institutions; but both for higher and lower reasons we all believe they should try also to correct and reform. I-imagine every member of this
house will agree with that statement. In the light of that, what are we to say to the fact that we have waited thirty-two years to deal with some of the things that were reported upon? When I read the act of 1939 it seems to me it deals in a purely mechanical way with great human problems. I can find only one section in this act which even attempts to deal with any human problem. Let me read one or two sentences from the last report and see if hon. members feel happy that this is the kind of thing to which we subject men.
