Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to go into many statistics, although I have before me a number of statistics, some of which have been referred to by the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Jaenicke). May I compliment him upon his maiden speech and the unusual ability he has displayed in delivering it. I join with the hon. member who has preceded me in the fine sentiment he has expressed, having had something to do for many years with the administration of criminal justice.
I wonder why it becomes necessary in 1945 to appoint a commissioner to investigate and ascertain whether the royal commissioners did in fact make the recommendations they should have made. In reality that is the position of affairs under this bill. The minister's predecessor and the minister .have carried some of them into effect, but many have not been touched and those that have not been touched1 are some that most materially affect the welfare of the men in the penitentiaries of this country.
The purpose of penitentiary reform should be to assist in turning social liabilities into social assets. I am not one who is ready to paint a dark picture because I have known of cases where unusual reformation has taken
fMr. Macdonnell.]
place. However, such cases are the exception rather than the general rule. I have in mind one case which I think should be brought to the attention of the house, for it illustrates what can be done when there are appreciative personnel trained to administer the penal laws with a degree of 'tolerance and fairness.
It is the case of a young man who was sentenced, following a conviction for murder, to the penitentiary at Prince Albert and he stayed there for fifteen years. When he en>-tered the Saskatchewan penitentiary he was eighteen years of age. The crime he had committed1 was the result of difficulties within the family, the sordid environment in which he lived. When he entered the penitentiary he was in grade 2. He stayed there until 1944, when through the instrumentality of an investigation made under the present Min-* ister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) he was granted a ticket of leave. AVhen he left the penitentiary he had an education equivalent to that of grade 12 or one year in a university. He joined the armed forces, achieved high non-commissioned rank and will shortly be discharged. He has informed me that he intends to go forth into the world with a desire to do something to tell young men in this country that crime does not pay. That is one example of reform in our penal system as it exists to-day.
Many of the recommendations made in 1939 not only have not been carried into effect, but no effort has been made to carry them into effect. Mention was made this evening by the hon. member for Kindersley of the terrible situation that exists with regard to juvenile crime.. This has been increasing by leaps and bounds. I think this is due in part to the failure of the government to implement the recommendations of the penitentiary report, particularly those with reference to the establishment of Borstal institutions in this country. The minister may say that that is a matter which might cause constitutional difficulty, but I ask him: What has been done between the dominion and the provinces to carry out recommendation No. 1 of the Archambault commission, which reads:
_ The Canadian penal system should be centralized under^ the control of the government of Canada, with the federal authorities taking charge of all the prisons in Canada, the provinces retaining only a sufficient number to provide for offenders against provincial statutes, prisoners on remand and those serving short sentences.
My information is that, following the publication of that report of the royal commission, most if not all of the provinces expressed a

willingness to permit the dominion, authorities to take over all reformatories within provincial jurisdiction. I may be asked what my authority is for making that statement. My authority is Mr. Justice McRuer, who was recently appointed- a judge of the high court of justice of Ontario and who was a member of the Archambault commission. Why has that recommendation not been carried into effect?
As I listened to the hon. member who preceded me I asked myself this question: Who is holding back prison reform in this dominion? Why has this matter been side-stepped and evaded over the years? I am informed that in 1939, following the publication of this report, the prisoners' aid society endeavoured to make personal representations to the Department of Justice but they were denied the opportunity of doing so. The failure to unify our penal institutions has resulted in conditions being such that in some cases juveniles entering the institutions graduate in very short order as high-grade postgraduate criminals.
Take, for instance, the spread of juvenile crime, referred to by the hon. member for Kindersley. The average number of major and indictable offences committed in Canada during the four years 1938-42 by those between the ages of sixteen and twenty-one years averaged 9,000 'a year. The proportion of young men entering our penal institutions is increasing. In 1936, of all the inmates in Canadian penitentiaries, nine per cent were under twenty-one years of age; in 1943 the figure was fifteen per cent.
Instead of something being done for the juvenile offender to give him a chance at rehabilitation through the establishment of a system analogous to the Borstal system, these young men are: being placed in institutions where they associate with old criminals. It . is all very well to say that there is some degree of segregation, but there cannot be sufficient segregation within one building to prevent old-timers from fully acquainting youngsters with all the secrets of the order to which they belong.
In respect of major crimes in 1900 there were 109 juvenile offenders out of every 100,000 of population in this dominion; in 1931, the number was 355 per 100,000 and in 1939, 469; or an increase of four times during a period of thirty-nine years.
In the matter of recidivists, multiple offenders, offenders returning for a second and a third time, between 1931 and 1942, of all the juveniles, youngsters between seven and sixteen years of ago, the number of repeaters
committing major crimes, not peccadilloes or unimportant infractions of the law, was thirty per cent; that is to say, three in every ten of those youngsters under sixteen years of age who had committed offences became repeaters in a period of eleven years. All this indicates to me that we in Canada are not doing our part by reeducation, by moral leadership, by moral suasion in our institutions to encourage these youngsters to an improved life. When we speak of reeducation I might point out that fifteen per cent of the juvenile offenders are described as illiterate. That condition demands that something must be done towards reeducating these boys and girls who commit offences. Yet there is no provision, no important provision to-day, to encourage education or to raise the standards of these young wrongdoers.
I am going to refer to the summary of the recommendations of the commission, some of which might have been earned into effect, some of which experience in recent years has shown should have been carried into effect.
I have already referred to centralized control. I refer to recommendation No. 6:
A planned reconstruction of the personnel of the penitentiary staffs throughout Canada should be effected in order that officers who have special training will be enlisted in the service.
There is a course to-day in that regard. It is a course that can be taken in one week. Visit these various penitentiaries and you find that there is no encouragement to efficiency on the part of the staffs to-day because of the limitation placed on their salaries. If we are to have the very best men possible for penal institutions parliament will have to raise the present rates of pay. The rates of pay for instructors run from $125 to about $175 a month. These rates must be raised if we are to secure the best possible men.
I come to recommendation No. 16:
A complete revision of the methods of classification of prisoners should be made, with provision for a thorough medical and psychiatric examination of prisoners.
Then No. 20:
All insane prisoners should be entirely removed from the prison population and treated in hospitals for the insane.
That is not being done. The minister says that there are no mental or insane prisoners in the penitentiaries. I will give an example. In Prince Albert penitentiary within the last year and a half there was a prisoner, and the warden had been warned that this man was insane. He paid no attention to that warning. Then a year and a half ago while the shoe instructor was locked up in a room

alone with this prisoner, the instructor was stabbed. The prisoner was then transferred to a mental hospital, Had the principles of this recommendation been carried out that man would have been removed from the penitentiary- to a mental hospital before rather than after the event. I am glad to have the support of the- bon. minister, knowing of his wide experience in the administration of -criminal law. He realizes, as do all hon. members who at any time have been for the prosecution or the defence, that the criminal code of this country is in very many particulars obsolete and out of keeping with present-day conditions and, the science of penology as it is known to-day. Take for instance the law with respect to insanity. We rely on the McNaughton case of ninety years ago,

a judgment delivered! before there had been the great advances made in psychiatry and the study, of insanity. We still follow the old principle in determining the insanity of a person charged with a crime in spite of the 1 results of scientific knowledge of the subject acquired in the last fifteen or twenty years.
Then there is the question of jurisdiction, and the other question of punishment, the amount of imprisonment that should be imposed. All these are matters that, deserve the serious attention of parliament. I realize full well that it will take a long time to reform the criminal code,. A year and a half ago I said in this house that I was sure that hon. members belonging to the legab profession would be only too glad of an opportunity, with such other hon. members as would be. willing to assist in a committee, assisted by the permanent employees of the Department of Justice, and after hearing in committee psychiatrists, psychologists, authorities on mental diseases, and the, like, in evolving a criminal code in keeping with present-day conditions. What we have been doing over the years is that parliament has added a section, and subtracted from another of the code of 1891 or 1892, with the result that to-day the criminal code is somewhat of a hodgepodge,. That would be a very large job, but there is no more important work which could be undertaken by this parliament; and I know the minister is in agreement with that viewpoint, We could begin at the next session of parliament. There are many committees, but this is one committee on which 1 am sure many hon. members would like to work. We would be doing something to reform the criminal law, to bring it u,p to daite, to remove obsolete elements and to take advantage of the scientific investigations ' which during recent years have helped to indicate some of the origins of crime and the courses to be taken with a. view of securing reform, all of which, of course, is .entirely foreign to the set-up of the criminal code1 as it now exists.
Sections 70 to 74 of the recommendations recommend, in the matter of adult probation, the setting up of a probation system modeled upoq the system now in force in England, for both adults and young offenders, and that probation officers recruited from the ranks of trained social service workers should be appointed by the courts. I suggest that in institutions where there are juvenile offenders, there should be established personnel guidance officers. I suggest, too, a midway institution for youth which is neither a gaol nor a penitentiary, but an institution where there will be full training in trade, inculcation of high moral principles, and leadership rather than

unnecessary coercion, with a view to changing the course of the lives of those young persons who have started on the road of crime.
Finally, I speak for the guards of these institutions. Some twelve years ago a change was made whereby guards for penal institutions were taken out of the operations of the Civil Service Act. Many of them are fearful that after years of service they will be removed and placed in a position where they will be denied pension benefits. I know full well that in recruiting men for the penal institutions there must be authority in the warden, with the right of appeal to the minister, to remove any officer who fails fully and efficiently to discharge his duty. But at the same time I feel that, first, there should be an increase in the salaries of guards in the penitentiaries to the level where we can secure better men than we have been able, in. the main, to recruit to-day. In our penitentiaries are many outstanding men who are giving their lives for low salaries because they are interested in the work. On the other hand some guards have taken the position because it is the. only available employment they can find at the moment. Let us recruit a higher standard of men who desire to do something to improve the lives of their fellow men. Let us have higher standards in the appointees to these institutions. Let us make it worth their while to secure positions in these institutions, and give the guards a higher degree of security than they now have. If parliament will act now, I am sure that five, six or seven years from now we shall be able to look back on the year 1945 and say that, having carried out the recommendations of the Archambault commission, we shall have succeeded in reducing the rate of increase that is apparent to-day among juvenile offenders, that we shall have caused a recession and that we shall have enabled many thousands of youngsters under the age of sixteen and other offenders between the ages of sixteen and twenty-one who have made a false step to start along the road to a new future, with a full appreciation of what their citizenship means to them, and a realization that the wray of crime does not pay.
Mr. JEAN -FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): The Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) and our colleagues have spoken like good Samaritans on a matter of general concern in this country. They deserve congratulations upon the high tone of their speeches; and while it is not wholly a pleasure, because the occasion is rather sad. it is a satisfaction to listen to a debate which is high above partisan politics.
. I do not well remember all that is in the report, but I read it when it was tabled, some years ago, and my first impression was that it was padded. One has only to look at the bioliography of the report to see the exaggeration of it, and to recognize that the report has been well padded in order to give the impression that the commissioners worked day and night on the matter. It is very easy to see that.
My first impression was that it was a bombastic report, intended rather to boost the commissioners than to help the inmates of penitentiaries; and my first observation to the then Minister of Justice was that, as a rule, when there is an investigating commission, it ends in an administrative commission on which all the investigators try to get good jobs. I make an exception for the father of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. MacdonneUl), who spoke very weld; also my hon. friends the members for Kindersley (Mr. Jaenicke) and Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker), who followed the fine example given by the Minister of Justice. I said to the then minister that I was concerned about one of the fellows who was on the first investigating commission; he wanted to be secretary of the other commission and the minister said in the house, "He will not be appointed." He told me in this house that no 'one who was on the investigating commission would be on the administrative commission. Another evening in the house, I remember, the then Minister of Justice, Mr. Lapointe, was tired. He came from my part of the country and I liked him very much. My hon. friend the member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) made certain observations similar to those -we have heard to-night. The question was asked, why was the commission not appointed? I believe it was in 1941, the year of Mr. Lapointe's death. I took the liberty, sitting behind the minister, of opposing the proposal, and the commission was not appointed. I had good reasons.
We hear a great amount of talk about bureaucracy-too much bureaucracy. Nothing is done by this house. And the snowball is getting bigger and bigger. A new commission! Everyone on the other side of the house complains about commissions, everyone complains about secrecy, and yet here we shall have another commission which will not be responsible to' this house. It will be like the radio commission, like the Bank of Canada; it will be like many other commissions. We shall have a report, but we shall not have the same facilities for obtaining information about what is going on in the penitentiaries as we have now when the estimates are before the

Penitentiary Aci

house and when the minister has to answer questions put to him from every part of the house.
I have a very strong objection on the ground that there is no responsibility. The thing is illogical, because one day hon. gentlemen complain that there are too many expenditures, that we must curtail expenses, and the day after they are all for something of this kind; they want to increase expenditures. They say, 'Go to it; the motive is good." I am opposed to administrative commissions and it is a matter of principle with me. I do not say this for the purpose of obstructing. I only repeat what I said at a time when the hon. gentleman who is now Minister of Justice did not ' discharge the functions which he is now called upon to discharge. At that time those functions were discharged by one of my dearest friends, my Quebec leader, and he thought there was something in my. views.
Moreover, the commission will cure no evil because it will be irresponsible. The hon. member for Lake Centre knows the mess that existed in Prince Albert owing to the incompetence of the warden. He was never dismissed. It reminds me of suggestions that have been made by some civil engineers for the repairing of wharves where the wood is rotten. They say, "Let us put another piece of wood, another board, over the board that is rotten and it will support the structure." When the warden is rotten, what is the use of having a commission? It will be simply a matter of whitewashing. The commission will serve no purpose.
If my hon. friend is dissatisfied with the state of affairs when the commission is established, and if he wishes to get information, he will then receive the answer that it is confidential information. Then we shall have motions in the house for the production of papers, for the production of copies of correspondence, et cetera. Hon. members will be told that the information which they wish to obtain is confidential information, and they will rise and ask for a vote and will say that the government is unfair to them and that we have no more democracy in this country. Yet this is what they are running after. Well, they will get only what they deserve if we have a commission. I repeat, it is most illogical and absurd from their point of view.
Let my hon. friends have the cpurage to ask for the dismissal of all wardens who are incompetent. Let them insist, not theoretically but in practice, that each warden shall be a man with a kind heart and a firm hand, a man of experience, a ma-n who shall not be selected by the civil service commission. The right man will never be selected by the civil service

commission but by the responsible minister after he has asked his friends to select the very best man for the job. There is no heart in the civil service commission.
I would say that a warden should be selected by a committee of clergymen of all denominations who know the man himself, who know that he has a generous heart but will not be fooled by the inmates. At the present time the inmates are pictured as saints or at any rate, as fellows who are ready to change their lives. My fear is not so much of those who have been in penal institutions. I fear for the coming generation that goes to the movies, that reads sensational stories, those who have never been in gaol. They can do anything. It is not the creation of a penal commission that will reform them. Such a commission will have nothing to do with them. Are my friends [DOT] credulous enough to believe that all criminal offenders are those who have been already in penitentiaries or in gaols? There are some recidivists, of course, but. not all of them are. Look at the record. They are not all like Lauzon and Peltier and the other fellow with a strange name- Koresky.	[DOT]

Well, he has his own record and his fingerprints must be in many places. I am talking about boys about whom everyone ought to be concerned. They are boys who belong sometimes to excellent families but who follow bad companions. Will this commission prevent such boys from going with bad companions? The commission will have nothing to do with them. It will have to deal with a small number of offenders, those who are recidivists. That is all.
Are my hon. friends ready to institute reform where it has to be made, right in the penitentiary? They are so naive, so credulous as to take it for granted that the establishment of a commission will be an improvement, and they are so sure of this that they will put the provincial gaols with the penitentiaries under the commission, when they do not know who will be appointed. Will the appointee be a third-rate lawyer running around here as a lobbyist through the corridors to get a job, or will he be a man of experience, wisdom and kindness? It will mean for him a life of sacrifice because he will have to look after those people. I know some wardens who come to Ottawa and who are as straight as sticks, going around thinking they are most important, that the world turns around them. The great Mr. So-and-so, the illustrious warden of such and such a place, who is infallible on the question of penal institutions. Everybody

Penitentiary Act
is naive enough to say how wonderful these men are, how disinterested; and when we ask for real reform nothing is done.
The first thing we have to do if we wish to bring about reform is to launch a campaign warning parents of the danger to which their children are exposed in these years. I do not say that those who complain of the present generation are right. Each generation hears the same story: "Well, in our time we were not so bad as the youth is now." Think of that, Mr. Speaker. With all the occasion that the youth of to-day have to do anything which is forbidden by the criminal code and by the other laws of the country, they are not doing so badly after all, and they deserve credit. Of course there is a criminal wave coming; it is only natural after a war when men have been led to kill each other, when human lives did not mean so much to the men, and when the object of those who had a rifle in their hands was to kill, and who made a sport of killing human beings as though they were killing game in the forest; it is only natural, but it could be much worse; and we may thank God that it is not any worse in this country.
I positively object to commissioes unless there is a reform, a long-needed reform', of those who are in contact with the criminals in those penal institutions. I remember very well

I do not think my hon. friend was here-when one of our lady colleagues received the humiliation of her life, here in this house, when she was making a saint out of a name, and the then Minister of Justice, Mr. Guthrie, took a paper from his pocket, read the report of that man who had committed many serious offences. It brought a great humiliation to our colleague who was sincere in advocating the rehabilitation of that man. Everybody remembers that. Those who were in the house-and my hon. friend the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) was one of them

remembers that. It is a most delicate matter; it is not a matter that can be dealt with by laws, commissions and regulations. It can be dealt with only by men -with their hearts in the right places. Not only the warden but the staff should be composed of men worthy of the warden, who should be an- exceptional man if we want some reform. If he is too good a man it will be an incitement to crime, because so many people will say that things are so well in the penitentiary that they must do something to go there as the unemployed sometimes break a window to go to gaol for shelter during the winter.
Of course opinions are free, but it is a dangerous game, and I warn the minister, who is an experienced man, to be very careful about all the intriguers who come to sell their skin, or I could put it otherwise, who come to ask for an appointment on that commission. I do not think the country has the means to establish a commission of that kind at this time, and I do not believe that commission would serve any good purpose. I would not be surprised if one of the commissioners, perhaps two or three, have been running as lobbyists in Montreal as well as in Ottawa to have the commission boosted, and then you would see them there.
I am a strong advocate of responsible government. So long as we have commissions we shall not have responsible government. There is no reason ini the world to establish *that commission. I do not say that to give the impression that I am grouching at the proposals which are made by ministers. They were made a long time ago, and I objected to them. I was sincere in objecting to them then, as I am now. I protest against it, and I believe that the members who favour it are just prejudiced or naive, and that the establishment of that commission will be another burden on the shoulders of the taxpayers of this country. I admit that my hon. friends who have spoken are sincere; they mean well, but there is no greater insult to a man than to say that he means well, he means well, he means well. That is no compliment. I do not say that to offend them, but I have had' a long experience in this house. I know the ins and outs of these things. I tell them to the house, and I think it is my duty to do so. I hope that they will think over what I have said as I have thought over what they themselves have said. I shall stop now because I want to listen to the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) before the sitting is over. He is a barrister of great experience, and I hope that he is not as prejudiced as our colleagues to whom we like very much to listen.

I am going to say something which I think is in disagreement with some of my colleagues, certainly something which is in disagreement with the hon. member for Kinctersley (Mr. Jaenicke). I begin by making this broad assertion, that in this House of Commons I know I speak on no subject with authority, but on this one I think I do speak with very considerable information. I have actively practised criminal law for thirty-seven years. Fourteen of those years were in the position of a prosecutor in Calgary. May I say to you people who live down here that it is an all-time job. Here you have a friend; he gets this court; the next one gets that court and you get the fees. I refused it on that basis and decided I must have a salary; otherwise I did not think I could discharge the duties of the crown. It will be remembered that we have no grand jury out there. Crown counsel take on that job for themselves and decide whether or not, after a preliminary hearing has been held, the man shall go on trial.
In this country from the beginning, punishment has been of a threefold character, or rather there are three phases of what we call punishment of prisoners who commit crimes. Number one is punitive. Number two is the reformation of the individual, and number three is that what happens might be a deterrent to others, that therefore society might be .protected. These are the three things all punishment seeks and that all penal institutions should1 endeavour to bring about. I am sorry to say that we in Canada confine ourselves to only two; that is, the punishment of the individual and the hope that his punishment may be a deterrent to others. It is rather a broad statement, but in this I agree very much with the hon. member for Kinders-ley, that in so far as reform in our institutions is concerned it is so negligible as to be not given a single thought. I have had instances of this kind, for example. A man may be given two years, or two years less one day; I have forgotten the distinction between a gaol and a penitentiary, but in any event I am only a day out-and I do not

mean from being an inmate. I have seen that man ask to be given another six months, and the magistrate or judge has obliged him. He asked for that because he had heard that in our penitentiaries he might learn a trade. With the exception of working in a laundry and perhaps making a boot or two, that is a complete fiction and absolute nonsense. Broadly speaking, we do not teach trades in our federal penitentiaries. So, as I say, of the three objectives we have in mind, certainly not more than two are in any sense carried out.	'
I am now going to say something in opposition to my great friend and seat-mate, to the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker) who sits in front of me and to the hon. member for Kindersley. I am anxious to put myself on record as saying that these people we get in penitentiaries are not all Sunday-school boys. There are bad men in this country. There is in this report a recommendation in connection with segregation, and so on, which in my judgment is the most important recommendation of all. I like this word "recidivist" or whatever it is; I used to call them repeaters in the simple place where I have lived for so long. I have handled the same men five or six times, and there was no object to be gained in their cases. And remember this, Mr. Speaker, that for the five or six times you get them, there are perhaps twenty times you do not. There are people in this world who are a menace to society, arid the sooner we get over these knitting group ideas that everyone we put in there has a halo around his head if we can but find it, the sooner I think we shall come to a more practical basis for dealing with these persons who commit crimes.
What happens in our courts to-day? A man comes up as a first offender, and what happens? Unless it be a very serious crime; he gets a suspended sentence. That is the invariable practice throughout the portion of the dominion that I know anything about; perhaps that is a very small section, but in any event it is large in area. Personally I am getting a. little fed up seeing twenty and twenty-one year old men, who can fight Germans and lick half a dozen old fellows like me, being constantly referred to in our courts as "this poor young boy who has gone wrong". He is not a poor young boy; he is a man. I got through university at nineteen. If anyone had called me . a kid I would have been ready to fight; so let us be a little bit practical about ages. The age of puberty is not twenty-one; it is a good deal less than that.

Penitentiary Act
Then what happens? A man is given this suspended sentence. He comes back again, and only then is he sent to an institution. Here is where I go along with hon. gentlemen to my left. I think the greatest criticism of all is that we have no place whatever to send them. It is easy to speak about segregating people in one institution, but those of us who know these places know it cannot be done in one place. My learned and hon. friend the member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) spoke a moment ago about individuals. I agree with all that, and I am coming to it in a moment; but to our great shame in this country we have no such places. Let us not divide ourselves into provinces or districts when we speak of moral and human responsibilities; but in the whole of western Canada there is not one place where we can send a youngster who has gone wrong, who we feel should not be at liberty for a while, where he would receive some discipline, some training, some instruction, and some religious teaching, if you like; I am all for it. We simply have no place where young people like that may be sent. There is an institution in Portage la Prairie, about which I know something. I know' the deputy attorney general of Alberta, having made a personal inspection of that institution a few years ago, stopped our youngsters from being sent there. He would rather have them sent to gaol, because they w'ould be better off. Certainly there is no room for that type of institution in an enlightened country such as this. I agree with what the hon. member for Kin-dersley said about the Borstal system. I have been reading and studying about it for years, but if I remember correctly, it does not apply to first offenders! I think the Borstal system applies only after the first offence, which is all the more credit to that system, because it has done some really amazing things.
Let us concentrate a bit. I appreciate the position of the minister in view of the first recommendation in the conclusion of this report, which appears at page 362 as follows:
In making the recommendations contained in this report, your commissioners believe that the government should gradually embody the recommended principles in a well planned programme. It is of first and immediate importance that legislation should be enacted to make provision for a prison commission, and that the members of the commission should be appointed at once.
May I say that I know the words "at once" have no application to the present minister. The date on this report is in such small print I cannot read it, but I believe it was made about ten years ago.
Upon appointment the prison commission should proceed to form well-ordered plans. . . .
Then it refers to Wakefield, in England, as something of an example. I can see that the minister will say he is carrying out the report -perhaps just a little bit late-and following that first recommendation in the conclusion. But when three of the best men we could possibly find, Mr. Justice Archambault, Mr. Dick Craig of Winnipeg and Mr. McRuer, now Mr. Justice McRuer of Toronto, have done all this, why in the world has another commission to find out whether or not they were right? Perhaps they formed their own little knitting group, or something of that sort, because many of their recommendations are of the sob-sister variety; they are nothing more than an expression of pious platitudes, and so on. But they have some real things in this report. We know the present minister is a humanitarian of the first water; so why should he not let us deal with this matter now as far as our jurisdiction goes? That is something beyond me.
I thought it was eleven o'clock, Mr. Speaker, but perhaps my eyes deceive me.

I am awfully sorry because I know that some of the younger men on the other side should be in bed before this; I am sure the older men can take it. I have just a word or two to say in conclusion. Let us in this country stop whittling at this thing. Let us cut down the old tree if it is necessary, but let us have something worth while.. Do not think for a moment that I am out of sympathy with the care, the nurture, the training and the teaching of which the hon. member for Kin-dersley spoke so eloquently. It is so much easier and so much more inexpensive to save someone who is going wrong than it is to pull him back up again after he has gone a long way down the hill. We all know that in our daily lives.
Therefore I simply make an appeal to hon. members. It may be that this is the start. I hate the idea of another commission. I disagree with the hon. member for Temiscouata. Even though he may not be able to get his handcuffs, I still think the business should be handled by some kind of commission, but not a commission of inquiry. I am sure that the Minister of Justice with his many duties has neither the time nor the inclination to take over a job like that.
I agree that most of the men we have operating our penitentiaries are men with army experience. That is my experience. I do not speak disrespectfully of them as individuals,
Penitentiary Act

but I know the hon. member was quite right when he said that discipline in a penitentiary or gaol should be of secondary consideration, that the man in charge should be a humanitarian. Do hon. members know that in Sing Sing in New York state an I.Q. test was taken and the inmates were one and a half per cent above the guards? That is a strange fact, but it is a fact.. What can we expect of guards to whom we pay $97.50 a month and then send them home in the evening to try to support their families. The only difference now between the guards and the inmates so far as I can see is that the guards are allowed to go home at night. That is just about the only difference we have in our penal institutions.
Let us not make two bites of this cherry. Let us do a job of work, not for those men who are gone and who must be segregated but for those who are coming up in this country. They can be saved. It is the smarties who are committing their first crime but who ultimately will become major criminals. They are not as dumb as most people believe they are. Let us leave out all these psychiatrists. There is only one thing I am sure of in connection with a trial for insanity; everybody is sure .the psychiatrist is crazy. In criminal law in this Dominion of Canada you do not need a psychiatrist to succeed with a defence of insanity. As one of our old English judges well said, a man is crazy when his friends think he is. That is much more solid reasoning in my judgment than having all these boys with these new degrees. It only began in the last war, this young science or art. We do not need these men with new degrees, with the long hair and staring eyes.
Motion agreed ho and bill read the second time.
